General-Purpose Digital Oscilloscope

A microcontroller oscilloscope I designed from scratch to answer one question: how much does the analog front end decide what a microcontroller's ADC can actually resolve? One board carries three acquisition paths so I can compare them directly.

Type
Personal project
Dates
Aug – Sep 2026
My role
Analog design, PCB, assembly, firmware, software
Board
2-layer KiCad PCB, hand-soldered
Controller
Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32
GitHub repository Try the auto-range simulation Read the math

1Overview

Problem

A general-purpose scope has to resolve signals that could sit anywhere in a wide voltage range. A fixed-gain front end forces a trade-off: a range wide enough to avoid clipping big signals wastes most of the ADC's resolution on small ones.

Approach

Build three acquisition paths on one board and measure how much accuracy each added level of design complexity buys: a simple direct read, a fully auto-ranging analog front end, and a high-resolution external ADC.

3Inside the auto-ranging path

Step 1 · Lift the signal into the ADC's range

The XIAO's ADC can only read 0 to 3.3 V, but a probed node can swing below ground. The first op-amp stage adds 1.65 V, so a ±1.65 V input becomes a 0–3.3 V signal that oscillates around a 1.65 V axis instead of 0 V. A unity-gain buffer makes that 1.65 V reference from a resistor divider, and the stage stays DC-coupled, because a series capacitor would strip the offset back off.

FIG 3-1 Level shifter, before and afterVout = Vin + 1.65 V
+1.65 Vlevel shifter→

Step 2 · Pick a window, then amplify it

After the shift, the signal goes through a chain of comparators. The first makes sure the voltage isn't too high. The rest form two windows nested around the 1.65 V axis: window 1 is 1.35–1.95 V (±0.30 V) and window 2 is 0.95–2.35 V (±0.70 V). An AND gate turns each pair of comparator outputs into a mux select line, and the mux sends the signal to the gain stage that stretches that window across the full 0–3.3 V ADC range. The comparators use hysteresis so the choice doesn't chatter at a window's edge.

4Comparing the three versions

VersionSignal pathResolutionDesign effortWhat I found
1V3 · External ADCRaw input → ADS8681 → SPI → ESP3216-bit nativeCustom SPI driver; split 5 V analog / 3.3 V digital suppliesMost accurate of the three.
2V2 · Direct ADCLevel shift → ESP32 ADC12-bit over 0–3.3 VSimplest: one op-amp stageSecond most accurate.
3V1 · Auto-rangingLevel shift → comparators → mux → gain → ESP32 ADCFinest steps near 1.65 V (up to 5.5× gain)Most complex: comparator ladder, logic, mux, two gain stagesSwitching op-amp gain stages caused delays and improperly amplified signals.

Takeaway: on paper, auto-ranging gives the finest steps for small signals. On the bench, the external 16-bit ADC beat it, and even the plain direct read did better, because the gain-switching stages added delay and amplification errors.

T1. Laplace transforms and the analog front end

The signal path from the probe tip to the ADC pins is linear: resistors, op-amps used with negative feedback, and the CD4052 switch, which acts as a resistor while it is on. The Laplace transform turns that circuitry into algebra. That algebra answers the two questions a scope designer cares about: how fast each stage responds to an edge, and what it does to each frequency. The window comparators and the mux select logic switch rather than amplify, so they have no transfer function. Their logic is covered in T4. Every number below comes from the schematic and the datasheets. None of it is a bench measurement.

T1.1 The transform in one page

The idea is to describe a signal as a sum of exponentials este^{st}est instead of as a function of time. Differentiating este^{st}est just multiplies it by sss, so a linear circuit's differential equations become polynomial equations in sss.

F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0−∞f(t) e−st dt,s=σ+jωF(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_{0^-}^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{-st}\,dt, \qquad s = \sigma + j\omegaF(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0−∞​f(t)e−stdt,s=σ+jω

Here ω\omegaω (rad/s) is the oscillation frequency and σ\sigmaσ (1/s) is the growth or decay rate. The property that does the work is the derivative rule. Differentiation becomes multiplication by sss, and integration becomes division by sss:

L{dfdt}=sF(s)−f(0−),L{∫0tf(λ) dλ}=F(s)s\mathcal{L}\left\{\frac{df}{dt}\right\} = sF(s) - f(0^-), \qquad \mathcal{L}\left\{\int_0^t f(\lambda)\,d\lambda\right\} = \frac{F(s)}{s}L{dtdf​}=sF(s)−f(0−),L{∫0t​f(λ)dλ}=sF(s)​

With zero initial conditions, each component's V-I law becomes Ohm's law with an impedance Z(s)=V(s)/I(s)Z(s) = V(s)/I(s)Z(s)=V(s)/I(s). Voltage dividers, nodal analysis and the op-amp rules then work unchanged on every stage of this board:

T1.2 The op-amp as a Laplace block (TSV794, IC1)

Across most of its useful range, a voltage-feedback op-amp behaves like an integrator: its open-loop gain falls at 20 dB/decade and reaches 1 at the gain-bandwidth frequency. Above its low-frequency dominant pole it can therefore be modelled as

A(s)≈ωts,ωt=2π⋅GBWA(s) \approx \frac{\omega_t}{s}, \qquad \omega_t = 2\pi\cdot\text{GBW}A(s)≈sωt​​,ωt​=2π⋅GBW

The feedback network returns a fraction β\betaβ of the output to the inverting input; 1/β1/\beta1/β is the noise gain. Substituting Vo=A (V+−βVo)V_o = A\,(V_+ - \beta V_o)Vo​=A(V+​−βVo​) shows that every feedback stage on this board is a single pole, with bandwidth equal to GBW divided by the noise gain:

Vo(s)V+(s)=A1+Aβ=1β⋅11+s/(β ωt),fCL=β⋅GBW,τ=12π β GBW\frac{V_o(s)}{V_+(s)} = \frac{A}{1 + A\beta} = \frac{1}{\beta}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + s/(\beta\,\omega_t)}, \qquad f_\text{CL} = \beta\cdot\text{GBW}, \qquad \tau = \frac{1}{2\pi\,\beta\,\text{GBW}}V+​(s)Vo​(s)​=1+AβA​=β1​⋅1+s/(βωt​)1​,fCL​=β⋅GBW,τ=2πβGBW1​

ST specifies the TSV79x family with a GBW of 50 MHz typical and 35 MHz minimum (RL = 10 kΩ, CL = 22 pF), unity-gain stability, a 30 V/µs typical slew rate and a 2.2-5.5 V supply. That characterisation table is for VCC=5 VV_{CC} = 5\,\text{V}VCC​=5V; no 3.3 V table was found, so the figures below assume the 5 V values also hold at 3.3 V. The VrefV_\text{ref}Vref​ buffer (section 1) has β=1\beta = 1β=1 and therefore gets the full 50 MHz.

Slew rate is a separate, nonlinear speed limit. H(s)H(s)H(s) only describes an output step whose initial slope ΔVout/τ\Delta V_\text{out}/\tauΔVout​/τ is below 30 V/µs.

T1.3 Level shifter (IC1 section 2)

The op-amp input draws only about 1 pA (ST typical), so R3 and R6 act as a 50/50 divider between the probe and VrefV_\text{ref}Vref​. R4 and R5 then give a non-inverting gain of 2. The halving and the doubling cancel, so the probe voltage passes through with gain 1 and is shifted up by VrefV_\text{ref}Vref​:

V+=R6 Vin+R3 VrefR3+R6=Vin+Vref2,Vls=(1+R4R5)V+=Vin+VrefV_+ = \frac{R_6\,V_\text{in} + R_3\,V_\text{ref}}{R_3 + R_6} = \frac{V_\text{in} + V_\text{ref}}{2}, \qquad V_\text{ls} = \left(1 + \frac{R_4}{R_5}\right)V_+ = V_\text{in} + V_\text{ref}V+​=R3​+R6​R6​Vin​+R3​Vref​​=2Vin​+Vref​​,Vls​=(1+R5​R4​​)V+​=Vin​+Vref​

With finite GBW and β=R5/(R4+R5)=1/2\beta = R_5/(R_4 + R_5) = 1/2β=R5​/(R4​+R5​)=1/2, both inputs pass through the same single pole. The final-value theorem gives H(0)=1H(0) = 1H(0)=1, which matches the ideal result above:

Vls(s)=Vin(s)+Vref(s)1+s/(β ωt)V_\text{ls}(s) = \frac{V_\text{in}(s) + V_\text{ref}(s)}{1 + s/(\beta\,\omega_t)}Vls​(s)=1+s/(βωt​)Vin​(s)+Vref​(s)​

For this board the numbers are:

  • fCL=0.5×50 MHz=25 MHzf_\text{CL} = 0.5 \times 50\,\text{MHz} = 25\,\text{MHz}fCL​=0.5×50MHz=25MHz, or 17.5 MHz17.5\,\text{MHz}17.5MHz at the minimum GBW.
  • τ=6.37 ns\tau = 6.37\,\text{ns}τ=6.37ns.
  • tr=14.0 nst_r = 14.0\,\text{ns}tr​=14.0ns, or 20 ns20\,\text{ns}20ns in the worst case.

A small probe step of ΔV\Delta VΔV starting from Vin,0V_{\text{in},0}Vin,0​ therefore produces

vls(t)=Vref+Vin,0+ΔV(1−e−t/6.37 ns)v_\text{ls}(t) = V_\text{ref} + V_{\text{in},0} + \Delta V\left(1 - e^{-t/6.37\,\text{ns}}\right)vls​(t)=Vref​+Vin,0​+ΔV(1−e−t/6.37ns)

This formula holds for steps smaller than SR⋅τ=30 V/μs×6.37 ns=0.19 V\text{SR}\cdot\tau = 30\,\text{V}/\mu\text{s} \times 6.37\,\text{ns} = 0.19\,\text{V}SR⋅τ=30V/μs×6.37ns=0.19V. Larger steps are slew-limited. A full 0-3.3 V swing takes 0.8×3.3 V/(30 V/μs)=88 ns0.8 \times 3.3\,\text{V} / (30\,\text{V}/\mu\text{s}) = 88\,\text{ns}0.8×3.3V/(30V/μs)=88ns (10-90 %), or 110 ns end to end. The full-power bandwidth for a 1.65 V-amplitude sine is SR/(2π⋅1.65 V)=2.89 MHz\text{SR}/(2\pi \cdot 1.65\,\text{V}) = 2.89\,\text{MHz}SR/(2π⋅1.65V)=2.89MHz.

Even a full-scale step settles within a few hundred nanoseconds, while one ESP32 conversion takes 10-20 µs. To the native-ADC paths the front end is effectively instantaneous. The flip side is that nothing in front of D0-D2 removes content above fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 (see T2).

T1.4 Inverting gain stages (IC1 sections 3 and 4)

Measure every voltage from the R24/R27 mid-rail Vref2V_\text{ref2}Vref2​. With the stage's mux channel on, Vmux≈VlsV_\text{mux} \approx V_\text{ls}Vmux​≈Vls​. With it off, no current flows in RinR_\text{in}Rin​, so the output sits at its idle level Vref2≈1.65 VV_\text{ref2} \approx 1.65\,\text{V}Vref2​≈1.65V. (As drawn, the nested windows select the unconnected Y3 whenever the input is inside window 1, so stage 1 may never be driven; see T4.) If both mid-rails equal VrefV_\text{ref}Vref​, a driven stage maps the probe voltage to its ADC pin as

Vout=Vref2−RfRin(Vmux−Vref2)=Vref−G VinV_\text{out} = V_\text{ref2} - \frac{R_f}{R_\text{in}}\left(V_\text{mux} - V_\text{ref2}\right) = V_\text{ref} - G\,V_\text{in}Vout​=Vref2​−Rin​Rf​​(Vmux​−Vref2​)=Vref​−GVin​

This is where the firmware's signed gains g1=−G1g_1 = -G_1g1​=−G1​ and g2=−G2g_2 = -G_2g2​=−G2​, and its offsets offb≈1.65 V\text{off}_b \approx 1.65\,\text{V}offb​≈1.65V, come from. The two mid-rails come from separate dividers (R1/R2 buffered, R24/R27 not). Substituting Vmux=Vin+Vref1V_\text{mux} = V_\text{in} + V_\text{ref1}Vmux​=Vin​+Vref1​ shows that the reference on the non-inverting input is amplified by the noise gain 1+G1 + G1+G, not by GGG:

Vout=Vref1+(1+G)(Vref2−Vref1)−G VinV_\text{out} = V_\text{ref1} + (1 + G)\left(V_\text{ref2} - V_\text{ref1}\right) - G\,V_\text{in}Vout​=Vref1​+(1+G)(Vref2​−Vref1​)−GVin​

Example, assuming 1 % resistors: the worst-case R24/R27 divider sits 16.5 mV low, which moves stage 1's offset by 6.5×16.5 mV=107 mV6.5 \times 16.5\,\text{mV} = 107\,\text{mV}6.5×16.5mV=107mV. If R1/R2 err 16.5 mV the other way, the offset moves by δ1+(1+G)(δ2−δ1)=16.5−214.5=−198 mV\delta_1 + (1 + G)(\delta_2 - \delta_1) = 16.5 - 214.5 = -198\,\text{mV}δ1​+(1+G)(δ2​−δ1​)=16.5−214.5=−198mV, about 0.20 V. CAL BANDS fits offb\text{off}_boffb​ and absorbs this offset.

Output range. The design gains are 3.3 V divided by the design window width, so each design window's edges land on the rails (stage 1 was sized for the earlier ±0.30 V window). With the R19/R20/R21 window-1 ladder (±0.275 V), stage 1 swings from 0.14 V to 3.16 V. Stage 2 swings from about 0 V to 3.30 V over ±0.70 V. That is wider than the ESP32's linear range, so only part of each window is usable. The firmware rejects any stage reading outside that range and falls back to the direct path:

Stage Output for its window Usable VinV_\text{in}Vin​, S3 (0.10-3.00 V) Usable VinV_\text{in}Vin​, C3 (0.10-2.45 V)
1, G1=5.5G_1 = 5.5G1​=5.5 0.14 V to 3.16 V -0.245 V to +0.275 V -0.145 V to +0.275 V
2, G2=2.36G_2 = 2.36G2​=2.36 about 0 V to 3.30 V -0.572 V to +0.657 V -0.339 V to +0.657 V

Negative inputs clip first because the stages invert.

Bandwidth. For an inverting stage the feedback factor is β=Rin/(Rin+Rf)=1/(1+G)\beta = R_\text{in}/(R_\text{in} + R_f) = 1/(1 + G)β=Rin​/(Rin​+Rf​)=1/(1+G), so the noise gain is one more than the signal gain:

When the mux connects a stage, its output jumps from the idle level by up to 5.5×0.275 V=1.51 V5.5 \times 0.275\,\text{V} = 1.51\,\text{V}5.5×0.275V=1.51V (stage 1) or 2.36×0.70 V=1.65 V2.36 \times 0.70\,\text{V} = 1.65\,\text{V}2.36×0.70V=1.65V (stage 2). That is well above SR⋅τ\text{SR}\cdot\tauSR⋅τ (0.62 V and 0.32 V), so the jump is slew-limited and takes about 50-55 ns. That is still far shorter than one ESP32 conversion.

Mux on-resistance. The CD4052B switch sits in series with RinR_\text{in}Rin​, so the stage actually sees Rin+RonR_\text{in} + R_\text{on}Rin​+Ron​:

G=RfRin+Ron=RfRin⋅11+Ron/Rin≈RfRin(1−RonRin)G = \frac{R_f}{R_\text{in} + R_\text{on}} = \frac{R_f}{R_\text{in}}\cdot\frac{1}{1 + R_\text{on}/R_\text{in}} \approx \frac{R_f}{R_\text{in}}\left(1 - \frac{R_\text{on}}{R_\text{in}}\right)G=Rin​+Ron​Rf​​=Rin​Rf​​⋅1+Ron​/Rin​1​≈Rin​Rf​​(1−Rin​Ron​​)

TI gives RonR_\text{on}Ron​ = 470 Ω typical (1050 Ω max) at VDDV_{DD}VDD​ = 5 V and 25 °C, and 180 Ω and 125 Ω typical at 10 V and 15 V. There is no 3.3 V specification. TI rates the part for a 3-20 V single supply and notes that performance degrades below 3 V, so 3.3 V is near the bottom of its range.

Estimate for 3.3 V: fitting Ron=k/(VDD−V0)R_\text{on} = k/(V_{DD} - V_0)Ron​=k/(VDD​−V0​) to the 5 V and 10 V typical values gives V0=1.90 VV_0 = 1.90\,\text{V}V0​=1.90V and k=1459 Ω⋅Vk = 1459\,\Omega\cdot\text{V}k=1459Ω⋅V. That fit predicts 111 Ω at 15 V (datasheet: 125 Ω) and about 1.0 kΩ at 3.3 V. The signal sits near mid-rail, where a CMOS transmission gate has the least gate drive, so 1-3 kΩ is plausible and higher is possible.

The switch current is at most 0.275 V/46.4 kΩ=5.9 μA0.275\,\text{V}/46.4\,\text{k}\Omega = 5.9\,\mu\text{A}0.275V/46.4kΩ=5.9μA in window 1. Stability check (based on assumptions). The model above treats the feedback network as purely resistive. In practice the inverting input has a few pF of capacitance CnC_nCn​ (op-amp input plus PCB, value not documented). That capacitance puts a pole in β(s)\beta(s)β(s) at 1/(2π(Rin∥Rf)Cn)1/(2\pi (R_\text{in}\parallel R_f) C_n)1/(2π(Rin​∥Rf​)Cn​).

For stage 1, Rin∥Rf=39.3 kΩR_\text{in}\parallel R_f = 39.3\,\text{k}\OmegaRin​∥Rf​=39.3kΩ. With CnC_nCn​ = 2 pF the pole is at 2.03 MHz, and with 5 pF it is at 0.81 MHz. Both are below the 7.7 MHz loop crossover. In the single-pole op-amp model that leaves only about 29° and 18° of phase margin. The level shifter, with R4∥R5=5 kΩR_4\parallel R_5 = 5\,\text{k}\OmegaR4​∥R5​=5kΩ, gets 43° and 28°. The likely result is peaking or ringing at MHz frequencies, and the op-amp's own second pole makes it worse.

There are two ways to deal with this:

  • Compensate it. Put a capacitor CfC_fCf​ across RfR_fRf​ with RfCf=RinCnR_f C_f = R_\text{in} C_nRf​Cf​=Rin​Cn​. This is the same RC-matching condition as the compensated probe in T1.7. For stage 1 it works out to 0.36-0.91 pF. For the level shifter (R4=R5R_4 = R_5R4​=R5​) it is Cf=CnC_f = C_nCf​=Cn​, or 2-5 pF.
  • Use it as a filter. A much larger CfC_fCf​ turns each gain stage into a first-order anti-aliasing filter, H(s)=−(Rf/Rin)/(1+sRfCf)H(s) = -(R_f/R_\text{in})/(1 + sR_fC_f)H(s)=−(Rf​/Rin​)/(1+sRf​Cf​). For example, 120 pF across R7 gives a 5.2 kHz corner.

The BOM lists no small capacitors, so neither option is on the board as drawn.

T1.5 ADS8681 internal anti-aliasing filter (U1)

TI places a second-order low-pass filter after the ADS8681's PGA, the same on every input range. The datasheet gives its magnitude and phase plots and two typical figures, −3 dB at 15 kHz and −0.1 dB at 2.5 kHz, but neither its Q nor its transfer function. The general second-order low-pass is

HAAF(s)=ω02s2+(ω0/Q) s+ω02H_\text{AAF}(s) = \frac{\omega_0^2}{s^2 + (\omega_0/Q)\,s + \omega_0^2}HAAF​(s)=s2+(ω0​/Q)s+ω02​ω02​​

A Butterworth shape (Q=1/2Q = 1/\sqrt{2}Q=1/2​) with a 15 kHz corner would stay within 0.1 dB up to 5.9 kHz, so it does not match TI's 2.5 kHz figure. Two equal real poles (Q=0.5Q = 0.5Q=0.5) match both figures. This README uses that model; it is a fit to two typical numbers, not TI's actual circuit.

HAAF(s)=1(1+sτ)2,∣HAAF(jf)∣=11+(f/fp)2,fp=15 kHz2−1=23.3 kHz,τ=6.83 μsH_\text{AAF}(s) = \frac{1}{(1 + s\tau)^2}, \qquad |H_\text{AAF}(jf)| = \frac{1}{1 + (f/f_p)^2}, \qquad f_p = \frac{15\,\text{kHz}}{\sqrt{\sqrt{2} - 1}} = 23.3\,\text{kHz}, \quad \tau = 6.83\,\mu\text{s}HAAF​(s)=(1+sτ)21​,∣HAAF​(jf)∣=1+(f/fp​)21​,fp​=2​−1​15kHz​=23.3kHz,τ=6.83μs

The consequences for this board:

  • Bandwidth. The 16-bit path has an analog bandwidth of about 15 kHz, even though the converter can sample at 1 MSPS. Inverting 1/(s(1+sτ)2)1/(s(1+s\tau)^2)1/(s(1+sτ)2) gives the step response 1−(1+t/τ) e−t/τ1 - (1 + t/\tau)\,e^{-t/\tau}1−(1+t/τ)e−t/τ: a 10-90 % rise time of 3.36 τ=22.9 μs3.36\,\tau = 22.9\,\mu\text{s}3.36τ=22.9μs with no overshoot.
  • Accuracy. 16-bit accuracy only holds at low frequency. The amplitude error stays under 1 LSB of the ±2.56 V range (78.125 μV/2.56 V=3.05×10−578.125\,\mu\text{V}/2.56\,\text{V} = 3.05\times10^{-5}78.125μV/2.56V=3.05×10−5) only below about 130 Hz. At 5 kHz the −4.4 % error is about 930 LSB on a 1.65 V-amplitude sine. For amplitude work above a few hundred hertz, divide by ∣HAAF∣|H_\text{AAF}|∣HAAF​∣ or calibrate at the frequency of interest.
  • Delay. The low-frequency group delay is 2τ=13.7 μs2\tau = 13.7\,\mu\text{s}2τ=13.7μs. In MODE ALL the firmware's z−1z^{-1}z−1 alignment only lines up sample indices, so the EXT trace still lags by this delay, about 0.14 sample at 10 kS/s, on top of any offset from the order of the reads.
  • Aliasing. At the default 10 kS/s the filter does not prevent aliasing. Nyquist is 5 kHz, but the filter is only 1.5 dB down at 10 kHz, so a 12 kHz tone folds to 2 kHz attenuated by just 2.0 dB. At 1 MSPS (Nyquist 500 kHz) the filter would be 53 dB down. T2 covers aliasing.

T1.6 Input loading: what the probe tip looks like

A bench scope presents 1 MΩ to ground. This board does not. IC1's V+ input draws almost no current, so R3 and R6 are in series from RawInput to the low-impedance VrefV_\text{ref}Vref​ buffer: RLSR_\text{LS}RLS​ = 20 kΩ to 1.65 V. On the ±0.625·VREF range, TI gives the ADS8681 input current as IIN=(VIN−1.6 V)/RINI_\text{IN} = (V_\text{IN} - 1.6\,\text{V})/R_\text{IN}IIN​=(VIN​−1.6V)/RIN​, with RINR_\text{IN}RIN​ = 1 MΩ typical (0.85-1.15 MΩ). Its input therefore looks like RINR_\text{IN}RIN​ to an internal 1.6 V, not 1 MΩ to ground. The Thevenin equivalent of the whole load is

RL=RLS∥RIN=19.6 kΩ,Vth=RL(VrefRLS+1.6 VRIN)=1.649 VR_L = R_\text{LS}\parallel R_\text{IN} = 19.6\,\text{k}\Omega, \qquad V_\text{th} = R_L\left(\frac{V_\text{ref}}{R_\text{LS}} + \frac{1.6\,\text{V}}{R_\text{IN}}\right) = 1.649\,\text{V}RL​=RLS​∥RIN​=19.6kΩ,Vth​=RL​(RLS​Vref​​+RIN​1.6V​)=1.649V

Connecting a source VsV_sVs​ with resistance RsR_sRs​ creates a voltage divider plus an offset. All three acquisition paths measure the RawInput node, so all three see

Vin=RLRs+RL Vs+RsRs+RL VthV_\text{in} = \frac{R_L}{R_s + R_L}\,V_s + \frac{R_s}{R_s + R_L}\,V_\text{th}Vin​=Rs​+RL​RL​​Vs​+Rs​+RL​Rs​​Vth​

When the source sits at 0 V, the board pushes 1.65 V/20 kΩ=82.5 μA1.65\,\text{V}/20\,\text{k}\Omega = 82.5\,\mu\text{A}1.65V/20kΩ=82.5μA (84.1 µA including the ADS8681) into the circuit under test:

CAL ZERO (input shorted, Rs=0R_s = 0Rs​=0) cannot remove these errors, because they depend on the source. Measure low-impedance sources (about 50 Ω or less keeps the error to 0.25 % and 4 mV), or put a buffer in front.

Open input. RawInput floats to Vth≈1.65 VV_\text{th} \approx 1.65\,\text{V}Vth​≈1.65V, the top of the range. (Modelling the ADS8681 as 1 MΩ to ground instead gives 1.618 V.) Each path then reads:

  • EXT: about +1.65 V.
  • DIRECT: Vls≈3.3 VV_\text{ls} \approx 3.3\,\text{V}Vls​≈3.3V clips the ESP32 ADC, so the reconstructed value is roughly the clip level minus 1.65 V: about +0.85 to +1.15 V on a C3 (readings saturate somewhere between 2.5 and 2.8 V) or about +1.45 V on an S3 (3.1 V limit).
  • AUTO: falls back to the direct reading, because that reading is outside both stage windows.

An unconnected probe therefore shows a large positive constant, not 0 V and not noise, which makes a handy bring-up check.

In the s-domain, cable capacitance CpC_pCp​ adds a pole at 1/(2π(Rs∥RL)Cp)1/(2\pi (R_s\parallel R_L) C_p)1/(2π(Rs​∥RL​)Cp​). With an assumed 100 pF and RsR_sRs​ = 10 kΩ, that pole is at 240 kHz. That is far above the 15 kHz ADS8681 filter and the 5 kHz Nyquist frequency at the default 10 kS/s (though not above the 500 kHz Nyquist frequency of the ADS8681's 1 MSPS maximum). On this board, input loading is mainly a DC problem.

T1.7 The compensated ×10 attenuator

Extending the ±1.65 V range means putting a divider in front of the input. A purely resistive divider fails at high frequency, because the load always has some capacitance. The classic fix is a capacitor across each resistor: a series arm Rt∥CtR_t \parallel C_tRt​∥Ct​ and a shunt arm Rb∥CbR_b \parallel C_bRb​∥Cb​, where CbC_bCb​ includes the input and cable capacitance. Each arm has Z=R/(1+sRC)Z = R/(1 + sRC)Z=R/(1+sRC):

H(s)=ZbZt+Zb=Rb (1+sRtCt)Rb (1+sRtCt)+Rt (1+sRbCb)=RbRt+Rb⋅1+sRtCt1+s (Rt∥Rb)(Ct+Cb)H(s) = \frac{Z_b}{Z_t + Z_b} = \frac{R_b\,(1 + sR_tC_t)}{R_b\,(1 + sR_tC_t) + R_t\,(1 + sR_bC_b)} = \frac{R_b}{R_t + R_b}\cdot\frac{1 + sR_tC_t}{1 + s\,(R_t\parallel R_b)(C_t + C_b)}H(s)=Zt​+Zb​Zb​​=Rb​(1+sRt​Ct​)+Rt​(1+sRb​Cb​)Rb​(1+sRt​Ct​)​=Rt​+Rb​Rb​​⋅1+s(Rt​∥Rb​)(Ct​+Cb​)1+sRt​Ct​​

The result has one zero and one pole. At low frequency the resistors set the ratio; at high frequency the capacitors do:

H(0)=RbRt+Rb,H(∞)=CtCt+Cb,H(0)=H(∞)  ⟺  RtCt=RbCbH(0) = \frac{R_b}{R_t + R_b}, \qquad H(\infty) = \frac{C_t}{C_t + C_b}, \qquad H(0) = H(\infty) \iff R_tC_t = R_bC_bH(0)=Rt​+Rb​Rb​​,H(∞)=Ct​+Cb​Ct​​,H(0)=H(∞)⟺Rt​Ct​=Rb​Cb​

When the two RC products match, the zero cancels the pole and the divider is flat at every frequency. When they do not match, partial fractions give a step response that jumps to the capacitive ratio and then relaxes to the resistive one:

vo(t)=ΔV[H(0)+(H(∞)−H(0)) e−t/τp],τp=(Rt∥Rb)(Ct+Cb)v_o(t) = \Delta V\left[H(0) + \big(H(\infty) - H(0)\big)\,e^{-t/\tau_p}\right], \qquad \tau_p = (R_t\parallel R_b)(C_t + C_b)vo​(t)=ΔV[H(0)+(H(∞)−H(0))e−t/τp​],τp​=(Rt​∥Rb​)(Ct​+Cb​)

As an example, take a ×10 divider into a 1 MΩ input: RtR_tRt​ = 9 MΩ, RbR_bRb​ = 1 MΩ, and an assumed CbC_bCb​ = 20 pF (an input plus short leads; a real probe cable adds tens of pF more). It needs Ct=RbCb/Rt=2.22 pFC_t = R_bC_b/R_t = 2.22\,\text{pF}Ct​=Rb​Cb​/Rt​=2.22pF:

CtC_tCt​ H(∞)H(\infty)H(∞) Edge vs. settled value Square wave looks
2.22 pF 0.100 0 % square (compensated)
2.60 pF 0.115 +15.0 %, decays with τp\tau_pτp​ = 20.3 µs spiky corners (over-compensated)
1.90 pF 0.0868 -13.2 %, recovers with τp\tau_pτp​ = 19.7 µs rounded corners (under-compensated)

Applying this to the board. The firmware command PGAIN DIRECT|EXT <g> sets the gain from the probe to the ADC node for the direct and ADS8681 paths. With a ratio-kkk attenuator, either set each gain to kkk times its calibrated value (DIRECT 1.0 becomes 0.1 for ×10), or recalibrate with the attenuator in place, in the usual order: CAL ZERO, then CAL GAIN with a known DC voltage at the attenuator input (it measures the product directly and overwrites PGAIN), then CAL BANDS so the gain-stage fits and windows are also referred to the attenuator input, then SAVE.

The divider cannot go straight onto RawInput, though, because the load is 19.6 kΩ to 1.649 V rather than 1 MΩ to ground. Two things go wrong:

  • Low input impedance. A ×10 series resistor would have to be Rt=9RL=176 kΩR_t = 9R_L = 176\,\text{k}\OmegaRt​=9RL​=176kΩ, giving an input impedance of only 196 kΩ.
  • The bias leaks through. Vin=0.1 Vs+0.9×1.649 V=0.1 Vs+1.484 VV_\text{in} = 0.1\,V_s + 0.9 \times 1.649\,\text{V} = 0.1\,V_s + 1.484\,\text{V}Vin​=0.1Vs​+0.9×1.649V=0.1Vs​+1.484V, so the usable source range becomes a lopsided -31.3 V to +1.66 V.

The workable arrangement is: a compensated divider to ground, then a unity-gain buffer, then RawInput. All four TSV794 sections are already in use, so the buffer needs another op-amp. The ADS8681 alone could accept ±12.288 V (its ±3·VREF range), but AIN_P is shared with the level shifter, so the range has to be extended in front of RawInput.

Trim CtC_tCt​ with a bench scope. In the example, the compensation error decays with a time constant of about 20 µs. That is shorter than one sample period at 10 kS/s (100 µs) and close to the EXT path's 23 µs rise time, so this board cannot show it clearly.

T1.9 Rise time of each complete path, and what the scope can resolve

Cascaded stages that do not overshoot combine roughly as a root-sum-square. The rule is exact for Gaussian step responses and a good approximation for chains of single poles:

tr,path≈tr,12+tr,22+⋯,f−3 dB,path≈0.35tr,patht_{r,\text{path}} \approx \sqrt{t_{r,1}^2 + t_{r,2}^2 + \cdots}, \qquad f_{-3\,\text{dB,path}} \approx \frac{0.35}{t_{r,\text{path}}}tr,path​≈tr,12​+tr,22​+⋯​,f−3dB,path​≈tr,path​0.35​

With the typical 50 MHz GBW of T1.3 and T1.4, and the ADS8681 filter model of T1.5:

Path Stages Rise time Bandwidth
V2 direct (D2) level shifter 14.0 ns ≈ 25 MHz
V1 stage 2 (D1) level shifter, then stage 2 (23.5 ns) 27.4 ns ≈ 12.8 MHz
V1 stage 1 (D0) level shifter, then stage 1 (45.5 ns) 47.6 ns ≈ 7.4 MHz
V3 ADS8681 internal filter ≈ 23 µs ≈ 15 kHz

A measured edge combines the signal's own rise time with the instrument's in the same way, so the true value can be backed out:

tr,meas≈tr,sig2+tr,scope2  ⇒  tr,sig≈tr,meas2−tr,scope2t_{r,\text{meas}} \approx \sqrt{t_{r,\text{sig}}^2 + t_{r,\text{scope}}^2} \;\Rightarrow\; t_{r,\text{sig}} \approx \sqrt{t_{r,\text{meas}}^2 - t_{r,\text{scope}}^2}tr,meas​≈tr,sig2​+tr,scope2​​⇒tr,sig​≈tr,meas2​−tr,scope2​​

To read within about 5 % without this correction, the instrument must be at least three times faster than the edge, because 1+1/9=1.054\sqrt{1 + 1/9} = 1.0541+1/9​=1.054.

Sampling sets the real limit. The GUI joins samples with straight lines (T2.8), so even a perfect step is drawn with a finite slope. A simulation of a sampled edge at many sample phases (not a bench measurement) gives these 10-90 % rise times, read from the straight-line trace:

  • An ideal step always reads 0.8T0.8T0.8T. A fast but finite edge reads between 0.8T0.8T0.8T and 1.6T1.6T1.6T, depending on whether a sample lands part-way up it.
  • A Gaussian edge with tr=3Tt_r = 3Ttr​=3T reads 0 to 9 % high (6 % on average).
  • With tr=5Tt_r = 5Ttr​=5T the reading is 0 to 3 % high.

A practical rule is therefore three samples on the edge:

tr,min⁡≈3T=3fst_{r,\min} \approx 3T = \frac{3}{f_s}tr,min​≈3T=fs​3​
Sample rate TTT Smallest edge measurable to about 10 %
10 kS/s (default) 100 µs ≈ 300 µs
≈ 22 kS/s (fastest AUTO, T2.10) 45 µs ≈ 140 µs
≈ 89 kS/s (fastest DIRECT, T2.10) 11 µs ≈ 34 µs

The native paths' analog rise times (14-48 ns) are about three orders of magnitude shorter, so on V1 and V2 the sample rate, not the circuit, sets the displayed rise time. On V3 the ≈ 23 µs filter only dominates once 0.8T0.8T0.8T falls below it, which happens above about 35 kS/s.

T1.10 Input protection: how much overvoltage the front end survives

Above ±1.65 V the level shifter clips at the rails. That protects D0-D2: an op-amp output cannot leave 0-3.3 V, so the ESP32 pins, the comparators and the mux only ever see in-range voltages. Only two things see the raw probe voltage: R3 together with the TSV794's non-inverting input, and the ADS8681's AIN_P.

The op-amp input has ESD diodes to VDD and GND. Model them as clamps at VDD+VDV_{DD} + V_DVDD​+VD​ and −VD-V_D−VD​, with VD≈0.5V_D \approx 0.5VD​≈0.5 V (assumed). Because V+=(Vin+Vref)/2V_+ = (V_\text{in} + V_\text{ref})/2V+​=(Vin​+Vref​)/2, a diode starts to conduct at

Vin>2 (VDD+VD)−Vref=5.95 V,Vin<−2VD−Vref=−2.65 VV_\text{in} > 2\,(V_{DD} + V_D) - V_\text{ref} = 5.95\ \text{V}, \qquad V_\text{in} < -2V_D - V_\text{ref} = -2.65\ \text{V}Vin​>2(VDD​+VD​)−Vref​=5.95 V,Vin​<−2VD​−Vref​=−2.65 V

Beyond those points, with R3=R6=RR_3 = R_6 = RR3​=R6​=R = 10 kΩ, the diode carries the current R3 brings in, minus the current R6 returns to the 1.65 V buffer:

ID=Vin−2(VDD+VD)+VrefR  (positive),ID=−2VD−Vref−VinR  (negative),PR3=(Vin−V+)2RI_D = \frac{V_\text{in} - 2(V_{DD} + V_D) + V_\text{ref}}{R}\ \ (\text{positive}), \qquad I_D = \frac{-2V_D - V_\text{ref} - V_\text{in}}{R}\ \ (\text{negative}), \qquad P_{R3} = \frac{(V_\text{in} - V_+)^2}{R}ID​=RVin​−2(VDD​+VD​)+Vref​​  (positive),ID​=R−2VD​−Vref​−Vin​​  (negative),PR3​=R(Vin​−V+​)2​
VinV_\text{in}Vin​ V+V_+V+​ Diode current R3 dissipation
+5 V 3.33 V (not clamped) 0 0.28 mW
+12 V 3.8 V 0.61 mA 6.7 mW
+20 V 3.8 V 1.41 mA 26 mW
−5 V −0.5 V 0.24 mA 2.0 mW
−12 V −0.5 V 0.94 mA 13 mW
−20 V −0.5 V 1.74 mA 38 mW

Three limits apply, and the tightest one wins:

  • Diode current. A typical 10 mA input-current rating (check ST's absolute-maximum table) is reached only near ±100 V.
  • R3 power. The PCB uses through-hole resistors. Assuming ¼ W parts, R3 limits the input to about +54 V and −50 V.
  • ADS8681. TI specifies input overvoltage protection to ±20 V on AIN_P with AVDD powered (check the absolute-maximum table; the limit is lower with AVDD off). This is the binding limit: about ±20 V with the board powered.

There are two side effects:

  • Rail injection. The clamp current flows into the 3.3 V rail. The XIAO's regulator can only source current, so the rail holds only while the board draws more than is injected. 1-2 mA is far below the ESP32's own draw.
  • Back-powering. With the board unpowered (VDD=Vref=0V_{DD} = V_\text{ref} = 0VDD​=Vref​=0), V+V_+V+​ clamps at about 0.5 V once the input exceeds about 1 V. A 5 V signal then pushes about 0.4 mA into the dead rail through R3. Do not drive the input while the board is off, or add a series resistor and Schottky clamps (that resistor then adds to RsR_sRs​ in T1.6).

T2. Sampling: from Laplace to the z-transform and the FFT

Every channel on this board turns a continuous voltage into a list of numbers taken every T=1/fsT = 1/f_sT=1/fs​ seconds. D0, D1 and D2 go through the ESP32's own SAR ADC, and the ADS8681 is read over SPI. This section starts from the Laplace transform and works up to the z-transform and the FFT, then applies the results to this board. It covers which input frequencies are safe at the default 10 kS/s and which ones alias, why the ADS8681 path behaves differently, how its one-sample pipeline delay is handled, and what limits timing accuracy. All numbers here are calculated from theory and datasheet typical values. None of them are bench measurements.

T2.1 Ideal impulse sampling

Model the ADC as multiplying the input by a train of unit impulses spaced TTT apart. The product keeps only the values at the sampling instants, but it is still a continuous-time signal, so ordinary Laplace tools still apply.

x∗(t)=x(t)∑k=−∞∞δ(t−kT)=∑kx(kT) δ(t−kT)x^*(t) = x(t)\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t-kT) = \sum_{k} x(kT)\,\delta(t-kT)x∗(t)=x(t)k=−∞∑∞​δ(t−kT)=k∑​x(kT)δ(t−kT)

A delay of kTkTkT becomes the factor e−skTe^{-skT}e−skT. The one-sided Laplace transform of the sampled signal is therefore a sum of delays, each weighted by a sample value.

X∗(s)=L{x∗(t)}=∑k=0∞x(kT) e−skTX^*(s) = \mathcal{L}\{x^*(t)\} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} x(kT)\,e^{-skT}X∗(s)=L{x∗(t)}=k=0∑∞​x(kT)e−skT

For this firmware, T=100 μsT = 100\,\mu\text{s}T=100μs at the default fs=10 kS/sf_s = 10\,\text{kS/s}fs​=10kS/s and T=50 μsT = 50\,\mu\text{s}T=50μs at 20 kS/s.

T2.3 The spectrum of a sampled signal repeats every f_s

The impulse train is periodic, so it has a Fourier series in which every harmonic has the same weight, 1/T1/T1/T.

∑kδ(t−kT)=1T∑ℓ=−∞∞ejℓωst,ωs=2πfs\sum_{k}\delta(t-kT) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{\ell=-\infty}^{\infty} e^{j\ell\omega_s t}, \qquad \omega_s = 2\pi f_sk∑​δ(t−kT)=T1​ℓ=−∞∑∞​ejℓωs​t,ωs​=2πfs​

Multiplying x(t)x(t)x(t) by ejℓωste^{j\ell\omega_s t}ejℓωs​t shifts its spectrum by ℓωs\ell\omega_sℓωs​. The sampled spectrum is therefore the original spectrum copied to every multiple of fsf_sfs​.

X∗(jω)=1T∑ℓ=−∞∞X(j(ω−ℓωs))X^*(j\omega) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{\ell=-\infty}^{\infty} X\big(j(\omega-\ell\omega_s)\big)X∗(jω)=T1​ℓ=−∞∑∞​X(j(ω−ℓωs​))

Once two copies overlap, nothing done after the ADC can separate them. The only cure is to prevent the overlap before sampling.

T2.4 Nyquist-Shannon and aliasing on this board

Nyquist-Shannon theorem. If x(t)x(t)x(t) contains no frequencies above BBB, samples taken at fs>2Bf_s > 2Bfs​>2B determine x(t)x(t)x(t) exactly. The folding (Nyquist) frequency fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 is 5 kHz at 10 kS/s and 10 kHz at 20 kS/s. A sinusoid above fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 does not disappear. It reappears at the alias frequency:

falias=∣f−ℓfs∣,ℓ=round⁡(f/fs)f_{\text{alias}} = \left\lvert f - \ell f_s \right\rvert, \qquad \ell = \operatorname{round}(f/f_s)falias​=∣f−ℓfs​∣,ℓ=round(f/fs​)
Input fff Alias at fs=10 kS/sf_s = 10\,\text{kS/s}fs​=10kS/s Alias at fs=20 kS/sf_s = 20\,\text{kS/s}fs​=20kS/s
12 kHz ∣12−1⋅10∣=2 kHz\lvert 12 - 1\cdot 10\rvert = 2\,\text{kHz}∣12−1⋅10∣=2kHz ∣12−1⋅20∣=8 kHz\lvert 12 - 1\cdot 20\rvert = 8\,\text{kHz}∣12−1⋅20∣=8kHz
19 kHz ∣19−2⋅10∣=1 kHz\lvert 19 - 2\cdot 10\rvert = 1\,\text{kHz}∣19−2⋅10∣=1kHz ∣19−1⋅20∣=1 kHz\lvert 19 - 1\cdot 20\rvert = 1\,\text{kHz}∣19−1⋅20∣=1kHz

An alias looks exactly like a real signal. At either rate a 19 kHz sine is drawn as a 1 kHz sine, the trigger locks onto it, and the host's frequency measurement reports 1 kHz.

Native ESP32 paths (V1 auto-ranging, V2 direct). Between RawInput and D0, D1 and D2 there are only op-amps and the CD4052 mux. No RC low-pass sits in front of the ADC pins. The intended band limit is the closed-loop bandwidth of each TSV794 section, roughly GBW divided by noise gain. ST specifies 50 MHz GBW and 30 V/µs slew rate (typical, at a 5 V supply; this board runs at 3.3 V, so treat them as approximate).

Stage Noise gain Closed-loop bandwidth
Level shifter 2 ≈ 25 MHz
Gain stage 1 (design G1=5.5G_1 = 5.5G1​=5.5) 1+G1=6.51 + G_1 = 6.51+G1​=6.5 ≈ 7.7 MHz
Gain stage 2 (design G2=2.36G_2 = 2.36G2​=2.36) 1+G2=3.361 + G_2 = 3.361+G2​=3.36 ≈ 14.9 MHz

For large signals, the slew rate limits a 1.65 V-amplitude sine to about SR/(2πA)≈2.9 MHzSR/(2\pi A) \approx 2.9\,\text{MHz}SR/(2πA)≈2.9MHz. Parasitic capacitance can lower these figures, but they stay in the MHz range. For example, an assumed 0.2 pF of stray capacitance across R7 = 255 kΩ would add a pole at about 3.1 MHz. The bandwidth of the ESP32's internal sampling network is undocumented, and this section assumes it is also far above fsf_sfs​.

Every one of these limits is roughly 500 to 5000 times fs/2=5 kHzf_s/2 = 5\,\text{kHz}fs​/2=5kHz. The native paths will therefore alias anything between fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 and several MHz, and noise aliases in the same way. Each sample carries the total noise of the whole MHz-wide analog bandwidth, folded into 0…fs/20 \ldots f_s/20…fs​/2. Sampling more slowly does not reduce the noise per sample. Only averaging or an analog filter does.

ADS8681 path (V3). The ADS8681 has a 2nd-order anti-aliasing low-pass after its PGA. TI gives two typical figures for it, valid on all input ranges: −3 dB at 15 kHz and −0.1 dB at 2.5 kHz. A Butterworth shape (Q=0.707Q = 0.707Q=0.707) with a 15 kHz corner would stay within 0.1 dB up to 5.9 kHz, which does not match TI's 2.5 kHz figure. Two equal real poles (Q=0.5Q = 0.5Q=0.5) at 15 kHz/2−1=23.3 kHz15\,\text{kHz}/\sqrt{\sqrt2 - 1} = 23.3\,\text{kHz}15kHz/2​−1​=23.3kHz match both figures, so this section uses that model. It is a fit to two typical numbers, not the actual circuit.

∣HAAF(jf)∣=11+(f/fp)2,fp=23.3 kHz\lvert H_{\text{AAF}}(jf)\rvert = \frac{1}{1 + (f/f_p)^2}, \qquad f_p = 23.3\,\text{kHz}∣HAAF​(jf)∣=1+(f/fp​)21​,fp​=23.3kHz
Frequency Role Model attenuation
5 kHz fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 at 10 kS/s −0.39 dB (×0.96)
10 kHz fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 at 20 kS/s; fsf_sfs​ at 10 kS/s (aliases to DC) −1.47 dB (×0.85)

At this firmware's 10 to 20 kS/s the filter corner lies above Nyquist, so it gives little protection against aliasing. A 12 kHz input sampled at 10 kS/s still reaches the converter at about 79% of its amplitude and appears at 2 kHz. A 19 kHz input arrives at about 60% and appears at 1 kHz. The filter also costs some accuracy inside the band. A 5 kHz sine reads about 4% low on V3, while at 1 kHz the loss is only 0.02 dB.

The V3 path rejects high-frequency interference and wideband noise much better than V1 and V2, about 26 dB down at 100 kHz. It is still not alias-free at the default rate. Under this model, 40 dB of attenuation at fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 would need fs/2≥232 kHzf_s/2 \ge 232\,\text{kHz}fs​/2≥232kHz, that is fs≥464 kS/sf_s \ge 464\,\text{kS/s}fs​≥464kS/s, far beyond a software-paced loop. Below that rate it is up to the user to keep inputs under fs/2f_s/2fs​/2. The alternative is to add an external low-pass filter.

Sizing an anti-aliasing filter for the native paths. For a record to be alias-free from DC to fpf_pfp​, every input between fs−fpf_s - f_pfs​−fp​ and fs+fpf_s + f_pfs​+fp​ must be attenuated, because those frequencies fold into 0…fp0 \ldots f_p0…fp​. An NNNth-order Butterworth low-pass with corner fcf_cfc​ gives

∣H(f)∣=11+(f/fc)2N,A(fs−fp)≈20Nlog⁡10fs−fpfc dB,N≥Areq20log⁡10((fs−fp)/fc)|H(f)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^{2N}}}, \qquad A(f_s - f_p) \approx 20N\log_{10}\frac{f_s - f_p}{f_c}\ \text{dB}, \qquad N \ge \frac{A_\text{req}}{20\log_{10}\big((f_s - f_p)/f_c\big)}∣H(f)∣=1+(f/fc​)2N​1​,A(fs​−fp​)≈20Nlog10​fc​fs​−fp​​ dB,N≥20log10​((fs​−fp​)/fc​)Areq​​

Take the default 10 kS/s and the 10-samples-per-period passband of T2.8, fpf_pfp​ = 1 kHz. The first folding band then starts at 9 kHz:

Filter Loss at 1 kHz Attenuation at 9 kHz
1st-order RC, fcf_cfc​ = 15.9 kHz (the noise filter in T3.5) −0.02 dB −1.2 dB
1st-order RC, fcf_cfc​ = 1.59 kHz −1.45 dB −15.2 dB
2nd-order Butterworth, fcf_cfc​ = 2 kHz −0.26 dB −26.1 dB

If the ESP32 ADC delivers about 9-10 effective bits (an assumption; T3.2), pushing aliases down to its noise floor (54-60 dB) takes roughly a 4th-order filter: two Sallen-Key sections per pin, which means another quad op-amp. A single RC mainly limits the noise bandwidth (T3.5). It does not make the native paths alias-free.

Charge kickback. The ESP32 has one SAR sampling capacitor CsC_sCs​, which is switched between D2, D0 and D1. In AUTO, each read therefore starts with CsC_sCs​ still holding another pin's voltage, up to about 3 V away. A capacitor CCC at the pin shares charge with it:

ΔVkick=ΔV CsCs+C≤LSB2  ⇒  C≥Cs(2 ΔVLSB−1)\Delta V_\text{kick} = \Delta V\,\frac{C_s}{C_s + C} \le \frac{\text{LSB}}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; C \ge C_s\left(\frac{2\,\Delta V}{\text{LSB}} - 1\right)ΔVkick​=ΔVCs​+CCs​​≤2LSB​⇒C≥Cs​(LSB2ΔV​−1)

CsC_sCs​ is not documented. For an assumed 5 pF and ΔV\Delta VΔV = 3 V the rule asks for at least about 40 nF, which agrees with Espressif's recommended 100 nF at the ADC pad. With 3 V of swing, 10 nF gives 1.5 mV of kickback (1.9 nominal LSB) and 100 nF gives 0.15 mV. To keep a 15.9 kHz corner with the larger capacitor, use R = 100 Ω and C = 100 nF, and take the op-amp's feedback from its own output, ahead of R, so that the loop sees a mostly resistive load at high frequency.

T2.5 Holding a sample: the zero-order hold

A sample-and-hold freezes a value and keeps it for one period. A DAC or a staircase plot does the same when it turns samples back into a waveform. "Hold for TTT" has a rectangular impulse response, u(t)−u(t−T)u(t) - u(t-T)u(t)−u(t−T).

Hzoh(s)=1−e−sTsH_{\text{zoh}}(s) = \frac{1 - e^{-sT}}{s}Hzoh​(s)=s1−e−sT​

On the jωj\omegajω axis this becomes a sinc-shaped magnitude droop and a delay of T/2T/2T/2. The factor TTT cancels the 1/T1/T1/T of T2.3.

Hzoh(jω)=T e−jωT/2 sin⁡(πf/fs)πf/fsH_{\text{zoh}}(j\omega) = T\,e^{-j\omega T/2}\,\frac{\sin(\pi f/f_s)}{\pi f/f_s}Hzoh​(jω)=Te−jωT/2πf/fs​sin(πf/fs​)​
f/fsf/f_sf/fs​ Example at 10 kS/s ZOH droop
0.01 100 Hz −0.001 dB
0.1 1 kHz −0.14 dB
0.25 2.5 kHz −0.91 dB
0.5 5 kHz −3.92 dB

The hold delay T/2T/2T/2 is 50 µs at 10 kS/s and 25 µs at 20 kS/s.

On this board, the stored numbers themselves are not drooped. Each conversion returns the value at its sampling instant, and the hold only keeps it steady while the SAR works. Droop and the T/2T/2T/2 delay appear only when samples are turned back into a causal staircase, and the GUI never does that with a waveform. It draws waveforms as straight lines (T2.8). It draws the band-code strip as steps centred on each sample: a centred hold with no T/2T/2T/2 delay, applied to a label for which droop has no meaning.

T2.6 The ADS8681 pipeline delay as z⁻¹

The ADS8681 samples and starts a conversion on the CS rising edge, but shifts the result out during the next SPI frame. The value read in frame kkk therefore belongs to the conversion started at the end of frame k−1k-1k−1. That is a pure one-sample delay:

yads[k]=x(tk−1)  ⇒  Yads(z)=z−1X(z),z−1∣z=ejωT=e−jωTy_{\text{ads}}[k] = x(t_{k-1}) \;\Rightarrow\; Y_{\text{ads}}(z) = z^{-1}X(z), \qquad z^{-1}\big|_{z = e^{j\omega T}} = e^{-j\omega T}yads​[k]=x(tk−1​)⇒Yads​(z)=z−1X(z),z−1​z=ejωT​=e−jωT

The delay has unit magnitude and a linear phase of −360∘⋅f/fs-360^\circ \cdot f/f_s−360∘⋅f/fs​. Left uncorrected, the ADS trace in MODE ALL would lag D2 by 100 µs at 10 kS/s:

Input frequency Phase error
100 Hz 3.6°
1 kHz 36°
5 kHz 180° (the two traces would look inverted)

The firmware primes one conversion before the loop. On every tick it reads the ADS8681, which returns the previous tick's conversion and starts a new one. It then reads the native pins and stores the ADS value together with the native readings saved on the previous tick. In effect the native channels also get a z−1z^{-1}z−1, so both refer to the same tick:

[ yads[k],  z−1ynative[k] ]=[ xads(tk−1),  xnative(tk−1) ]\big[\,y_{\text{ads}}[k],\; z^{-1}y_{\text{native}}[k]\,\big] = \big[\,x_{\text{ads}}(t_{k-1}),\; x_{\text{native}}(t_{k-1})\,\big][yads​[k],z−1ynative​[k]]=[xads​(tk−1​),xnative​(tk−1​)]

Two sub-sample skews remain, both estimates. Within a tick the native reads follow the CS edge one after another, each on the order of 10 to 20 µs. In addition, the ADS8681's filter delays the signal by its group delay, 2/(2πfp)≈14 μs2/(2\pi f_p) \approx 14\,\mu\text{s}2/(2πfp​)≈14μs at low frequency for the Q = 0.5 model (−4.9° at 1 kHz). Both make the ADS trace lag, so they add. A total skew Δt\Delta tΔt of 10, 20 or 50 µs gives a phase error 360∘fΔt360^\circ f\Delta t360∘fΔt of 3.6°, 7.2° or 18° at 1 kHz.

The AUTO path has its own, separate timing, which concerns D2 versus the gain-stage pins, not the ADS8681. Every AUTO sample uses the same read sequence: x0x_0x0​ = D2, then each enabled stage (stage 1 in slot 1, stage 2 in slot 2), then x1x_1x1​ = D2 in slot 3. Each stage reading is checked against the direct reading interpolated to its own slot, which cancels the first-order (linear-in-time) skew (T4.5). The value AUTO stores comes from the read that produced it: slot 0 for band 0, slot 1 for stage 1, slot 2 for stage 2. The AUTO trace's effective sampling instant therefore steps by one or two read times (roughly 10 to 40 µs) when the band changes. The step is the same every time for a given band. Correcting it would mean subtracting a slope estimated from the D2 reads, which would add the direct path's noise back into the stage readings and cancel their advantage.

T2.7 DTFT, DFT and FFT: what a spectrum view would show

Evaluating X(z)X(z)X(z) on the unit circle, z=ejΩz = e^{j\Omega}z=ejΩ, gives the discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT). It repeats every 2π2\pi2π in Ω\OmegaΩ, which is every fsf_sfs​ in hertz: the same image structure as in T2.3.

X(ejΩ)=∑kx[k] e−jΩk,Ω=2πf/fsX(e^{j\Omega}) = \sum_{k} x[k]\,e^{-j\Omega k}, \qquad \Omega = 2\pi f/f_sX(ejΩ)=k∑​x[k]e−jΩk,Ω=2πf/fs​

A record holds only nnn samples. The DFT samples the DTFT of the windowed record at nnn equally spaced frequencies. The FFT computes it in O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) operations instead of O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2).

X[m]=∑k=0n−1w[k] x[k] e−j2πmk/n,fm=m fsn,m=0,…,n/2X[m] = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} w[k]\,x[k]\,e^{-j2\pi mk/n}, \qquad f_m = m\,\frac{f_s}{n}, \quad m = 0,\dots,n/2X[m]=k=0∑n−1​w[k]x[k]e−j2πmk/n,fm​=mnfs​​,m=0,…,n/2

The bin spacing is Δf=fs/n=1/(nT)\Delta f = f_s/n = 1/(nT)Δf=fs​/n=1/(nT), one over the record duration.

nnn Record at 10 kS/s Δf\Delta fΔf at 10 kS/s Record at 20 kS/s Δf\Delta fΔf at 20 kS/s
1000 (default) 0.1 s 10 Hz 0.05 s 20 Hz
4096 (maximum) 0.4096 s 2.44 Hz 0.2048 s 4.88 Hz

Leakage. The DFT treats the record as one period of a repeating signal. If the record does not hold a whole number of cycles, the jump where it wraps around spreads energy into every bin. Take two synthetic, noise-free tones at 10 kS/s with n=1000n = 1000n=1000. A 1000 Hz tone is exactly 100 cycles and lands entirely in bin 100. A 1005 Hz tone is 100.5 cycles, the worst case. With no window, the bins 10 away from its peak are only about −26 dB down, and at 2 kHz the leakage is −43 to −49 dB, depending on the tone's phase.

A Hann window tapers the record towards zero at both ends. The equation below is the periodic form. numpy.hanning(n) puts n−1n-1n−1 in the denominator instead, which makes a negligible difference at this length.

w[k]=12(1−cos⁡2πkn),k=0,…,n−1w[k] = \tfrac12\left(1 - \cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right), \qquad k = 0,\dots,n-1w[k]=21​(1−cosn2πk​),k=0,…,n−1

With Hann, the same 1005 Hz tone is about −70 dB down 10 bins from the peak and about −129 dB down at 2 kHz, far below any ADC noise floor. The price is a wider main lobe and a lower amplitude, which must be corrected.

Property Rectangular (no window) Hann
Highest sidelobe −13.3 dB −31.5 dB
Main lobe, null to null 2 bins 4 bins
Equivalent noise bandwidth (ENBW) 1.00 bin 1.50 bins
Worst-case scalloping loss (tone halfway between bins) −3.92 dB −1.42 dB
Coherent gain 1n∑w[k]\tfrac1n\sum w[k]n1​∑w[k] 1.0 0.5

For a tone centred on bin mmm, its amplitude is A≈2∣X[m]∣/∑kw[k]A \approx 2\lvert X[m]\rvert / \sum_k w[k]A≈2∣X[m]∣/∑k​w[k]. A tone between bins reads low by up to the scalloping loss. For white noise, each bin holds only ENBW/(n/2)\text{ENBW}/(n/2)ENBW/(n/2) of the total noise power. The FFT noise floor therefore sits 10log⁡10(n/(2 ENBW))10\log_{10}\big(n/(2\,\text{ENBW})\big)10log10​(n/(2ENBW)) below the total noise: 27.0 dB (rectangular) or 25.2 dB (Hann) for n=1000n = 1000n=1000, and 33.1 dB or 31.4 dB for n=4096n = 4096n=4096.

The GUI has no FFT view yet, so this subsection describes what one would show. numpy.fft.rfft(x*w) accepts any nnn, including 1000. Only 0 to fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 is meaningful. An alias appears as an ordinary-looking peak, and the FFT cannot flag it.

T2.8 Reconstruction for display: sinc vs straight lines

The ideal reconstruction (Whittaker-Shannon) applies an ideal low-pass at fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 (gain TTT) to the impulse train. It is exact for a band-limited input with fs>2Bf_s > 2Bfs​>2B, but it needs every sample, past and future. In practice it is approximated with a windowed sinc or with FFT zero-padding.

x(t)=∑kx[k] sinc⁡ ⁣(t−kTT),sinc⁡(u)=sin⁡πuπux(t) = \sum_{k} x[k]\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t - kT}{T}\right), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin \pi u}{\pi u}x(t)=k∑​x[k]sinc(Tt−kT​),sinc(u)=πusinπu​

The GUI plot instead joins the samples with straight lines. That is linear interpolation: a triangular kernel, two samples wide, whose baseband response is sinc⁡2(f/fs)\operatorname{sinc}^2(f/f_s)sinc2(f/fs​). It gives −0.29 dB at 0.1fs0.1f_s0.1fs​, −1.82 dB at 0.25fs0.25f_s0.25fs​ and −7.84 dB at fs/2f_s/2fs​/2, and leaves attenuated images that show up as corners in the trace.

The time domain makes this more concrete. Take a sine with MMM samples per period. The worst case is a peak that falls midway between two samples, and the drawn line then tops out at Acos⁡(π/M)A\cos(\pi/M)Acos(π/M):

ΔAA=1−cos⁡πM≈π22M2\frac{\Delta A}{A} = 1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{M} \approx \frac{\pi^2}{2M^2}AΔA​=1−cosMπ​≈2M2π2​
MMM (samples per period) Worst-case peak error
4 29%
10 4.9%
20 1.2%

This is where the rule of thumb of about 10 samples per period for a faithful-looking trace comes from. It means up to 1 kHz at 10 kS/s and 2 kHz at 20 kS/s. Between that limit and fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 the samples are still valid (nothing aliases), but the line plot looks jagged.

The host's min, max and pk-pk values come from the raw samples, so a peak can read low by up to A(1−cos⁡(π/M))A(1-\cos(\pi/M))A(1−cos(π/M)). This worst case occurs when the sample phases repeat every period, for example when fsf_sfs​ is an exact multiple of fff. Otherwise the phases drift over a long record, some sample lands close to the true peak, and the error shrinks.

T2.9 Real-time vs equivalent-time sampling

Real-time sampling (this scope). Every sample of a record comes from one acquisition, so fsf_sfs​ itself must satisfy Nyquist for the signal. This is what allows one-shot events to be captured.

Equivalent-time sampling. For a strictly repetitive signal, a scope can take a few samples per trigger, shift the delay by Δt\Delta tΔt on each trigger, and assemble the pieces. The effective rate is 1/Δt1/\Delta t1/Δt. For example, 100 points per period of a 50 kHz signal needs Δt=200 ns\Delta t = 200\,\text{ns}Δt=200ns (an effective 5 MS/s).

That only works if the trigger-to-sample delay is known to a small fraction of Δt\Delta tΔt. Here the trigger is found in software from the samples themselves, and timing uncertainty is at the µs level (T2.10), so this design cannot do it.

T2.10 Sample timing, measured rate and jitter

Pacing. The firmware busy-waits on the CPU cycle counter, with a period of ⌊fclk/fs⌋\lfloor f_{\text{clk}}/f_s \rfloor⌊fclk​/fs​⌋ cycles. The clock frequencies below are assumed Arduino-core defaults. The firmware reads the actual value at run time.

CPU clock (assumed default) One cycle Cycles per sample at 10 kS/s
160 MHz (C3, C6) 6.25 ns 16000
240 MHz (S3) 4.17 ns 24000

Rounding the period to whole cycles has a negligible effect. For example, 7 kS/s at 160 MHz becomes 22857 cycles, or 7000.04 S/s (+6.25 ppm).

Every sample in a given mode costs the same fixed sequence of reads: one native read for DIRECT, four for AUTO with both stages enabled (D2, D0, D1, D2), and an ADS8681 SPI frame added for EXT and MODE ALL. Before each capture the firmware times four dry-run samples and never paces faster than the slowest one plus 12.5 % margin. At an assumed 10 to 20 µs per read, AUTO therefore runs at up to about 11 to 22 kS/s, and DIRECT at up to about 44 to 89 kS/s. Asking for more gives evenly spaced samples at the achievable rate, not unevenly spaced ones. An interrupt can still delay an individual sample; the loop then shortens the next interval to get back on the grid, unless it has fallen more than a whole period behind. The firmware measures the rate it actually achieved and sends it with the frame. It counts all nacqn_\text{acq}nacq​ samples of the acquisition, including those overwritten in the ring while waiting for the trigger (T4.9), which span nacq−1n_\text{acq} - 1nacq​−1 intervals:

f^s=nacq−1tlast−tfirst\hat f_s = \frac{n_\text{acq} - 1}{t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{first}}}f^​s​=tlast​−tfirst​nacq​−1​

With 1 µs timestamps over a span of at least 99.9 ms (a 1000-sample record at 10 kS/s), timestamp resolution contributes at most 10 ppm. The timestamps and the cycle counter both run from the board's crystal, so f^s\hat f_sf^​s​ cannot detect the crystal's own frequency error (assumed to be tens of ppm). That error remains as a small scale error on the time axis. f^s\hat f_sf^​s​ is also an average, so it does not show the occasional interrupt-delayed sample.

Jitter. Suppose each sampling instant has a random error with rms value σt\sigma_tσt​. The voltage error is then approximately the signal's slope times the timing error. For a sine of amplitude AAA, the rms slope is 2πfA/22\pi f A/\sqrt22πfA/2​ and the rms signal is A/2A/\sqrt2A/2​, so AAA cancels:

SNRjitter=−20log⁡10 ⁣(2πfin σt) dB,ENOB=SNR−1.766.02\text{SNR}_{\text{jitter}} = -20\log_{10}\!\left(2\pi f_{\text{in}}\,\sigma_t\right)\ \text{dB}, \qquad \text{ENOB} = \frac{\text{SNR} - 1.76}{6.02}SNRjitter​=−20log10​(2πfin​σt​) dB,ENOB=6.02SNR−1.76​

The two values of σt\sigma_tσt​ below are assumptions that bracket the timing; neither has been measured. 0.1 µs represents a tight spin loop. 1 µs represents software pacing disturbed by interrupts such as the RTOS tick or USB. Occasional interrupt delays of many µs act more like isolated glitches than like Gaussian jitter.

finf_{\text{in}}fin​ σt=0.1 μs\sigma_t = 0.1\,\mu\text{s}σt​=0.1μs σt=1 μs\sigma_t = 1\,\mu\text{s}σt​=1μs
100 Hz 84.0 dB, 13.7 bits 64.0 dB, 10.3 bits
1 kHz 64.0 dB, 10.3 bits 44.0 dB, 7.0 bits
10 kHz (needs fs>20 kS/sf_s > 20\,\text{kS/s}fs​>20kS/s) 44.0 dB, 7.0 bits 24.0 dB, 3.7 bits

For comparison, the ideal quantization SNR 6.02N+1.766.02N + 1.766.02N+1.76 is 74.0 dB for N=12N = 12N=12 (ESP32) and 98.1 dB for N=16N = 16N=16 (ADS8681). With 1 µs of jitter, a full-scale 1 kHz sine is limited to about 7 effective bits, whichever ADC converts it.

In volts, a 1 µs timing error on a 1.65 V-amplitude 1 kHz sine produces up to 2πfA δt=10.4 mV2\pi f A\,\delta t = 10.4\,\text{mV}2πfAδt=10.4mV (7.3 mV rms for σt=1 μs\sigma_t = 1\,\mu\text{s}σt​=1μs). That is about 10 times the 1 mV resolution of analogReadMilliVolts() and about 133 ADS8681 LSBs (78.125 µV each). The ADS8681's 16 bits therefore pay off only for slow signals, or if its conversions were timed by hardware, for example with CS driven by a timer peripheral. The converter's own aperture jitter was not looked up for this section and is assumed to be negligible next to software jitter.

T3. Resolution and noise

Two different things limit the smallest voltage this scope can resolve. Quantization is deterministic: the ADC rounds every sample to the nearest code, so there is a step size below which nothing is visible. Noise is random: resistors, op-amps, the sampling capacitor and the supply all add a fluctuating voltage that makes the code jump around even with a perfectly still input. A path is only as good as the larger of the two. Every number in this section is a design or datasheet estimate, not a bench measurement.

T3.1 Quantization step and quantization noise

An NNN-bit ADC divides its full-scale range (FSR) into 2N2^N2N equal steps. The step size is the smallest change the ADC can report, so it sets the resolution of each path.

LSB=FSR2N\text{LSB} = \frac{\text{FSR}}{2^N}LSB=2NFSR​
Converter FSR NNN LSB σq=LSB/12\sigma_q = \text{LSB}/\sqrt{12}σq​=LSB/12​
ESP32 ADC, nominal 3.3 V/40963.3\,\text{V}/40963.3V/4096 3.3 V 12 805.7 µV 232.6 µV
analogReadMilliVolts() result (integer mV) n/a n/a 1 mV 288.7 µV
ADS8681, range code 0x4 (±0.625 VREF=±2.56 V\pm 0.625\,V_{\text{REF}} = \pm 2.56\,\text{V}±0.625VREF​=±2.56V) 5.12 V 16 78.125 µV 22.55 µV

Three practical notes for the native path:

  • The true code step depends on the chip. At the highest attenuation the voltage at code 4095 is set by the chip's internal reference (1.0 to 1.2 V from chip to chip, per Espressif) times the attenuation, not by VDD. One ESP32-C3 user reports code 4095 at about 2.8 V, which is about 0.68 mV per code. This section uses the nominal 805.7 µV.
  • The reported step is 1 mV. analogReadMilliVolts() returns an integer number of millivolts, so the firmware only ever sees 1 mV steps. This second quantizer is slightly coarser than the nominal code step.
  • The calibrated span is narrower than 0 to 3.3 V. Espressif's ESP-IDF v4.4 pages give 0 to 2500 mV for the ESP32-C3 and 0 to 3100 mV for the ESP32-S3 at the highest attenuation. Espressif's 2025 ADC comparison article lists about 0 to 2900 mV for the S3. If a C6 is fitted, check its datasheet. On a C3 the direct path therefore saturates at Vls=2.5 VV_{\text{ls}} = 2.5\,\text{V}Vls​=2.5V, i.e. Vin=+0.85 VV_{\text{in}} = +0.85\,\text{V}Vin​=+0.85V, not +1.65 V. The inverting stages also clip for negative inputs. A C3 build of the firmware therefore treats stage readings above 2.45 V (instead of 3.00 V) as clipped, so it uses stage 1 only above Vin=−0.145 VV_{\text{in}} = -0.145\,\text{V}Vin​=−0.145V and stage 2 only above −0.339 V-0.339\,\text{V}−0.339V.

Why 12\sqrt{12}12​: if the input is "busy" (it moves by many LSBs between samples, or carries noise larger than about half an LSB), the rounding error eee is equally likely to be anywhere in [−LSB/2,+LSB/2][-\text{LSB}/2, +\text{LSB}/2][−LSB/2,+LSB/2]. Its probability density is the constant 1/LSB1/\text{LSB}1/LSB, and its variance is

σq2=∫−LSB/2+LSB/2e2 1LSB de=1LSB[e33]−LSB/2+LSB/2=LSB212⇒σq=LSB12≈0.289 LSB\sigma_q^2 = \int_{-\text{LSB}/2}^{+\text{LSB}/2} e^2\,\frac{1}{\text{LSB}}\,de = \frac{1}{\text{LSB}}\left[\frac{e^3}{3}\right]_{-\text{LSB}/2}^{+\text{LSB}/2} = \frac{\text{LSB}^2}{12} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \sigma_q = \frac{\text{LSB}}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.289\,\text{LSB}σq2​=∫−LSB/2+LSB/2​e2LSB1​de=LSB1​[3e3​]−LSB/2+LSB/2​=12LSB2​⇒σq​=12​LSB​≈0.289LSB

The uniform model fails for a perfectly clean DC input, because the error is then a fixed offset, not noise. It becomes accurate once the analog noise is about 0.5 LSB rms or more: with 0.5 LSB of Gaussian noise the average error of the quantizer is below 0.003 LSB. The ADS8681's datasheet noise is about 0.7 LSB rms (see below). The ESP32's own noise is expected to be larger than 1 LSB, but it has to be measured.

T3.2 Ideal SQNR and ENOB

The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio compares a full-scale sine with σq\sigma_qσq​. A full-scale sine has amplitude FSR/2=2N LSB/2\text{FSR}/2 = 2^{N}\,\text{LSB}/2FSR/2=2NLSB/2 and RMS value 2N LSB/(22)2^{N}\,\text{LSB}/(2\sqrt{2})2NLSB/(22​):

SQNR=20log⁡102N LSB/(22)LSB/12=20log⁡10 ⁣(2N32)=N⋅20log⁡102+20log⁡101.5=6.02 N+1.76 dB\text{SQNR} = 20\log_{10}\frac{2^{N}\,\text{LSB}/(2\sqrt{2})}{\text{LSB}/\sqrt{12}} = 20\log_{10}\!\left(2^{N}\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{2}}\right) = N\cdot 20\log_{10}2 + 20\log_{10}\sqrt{1.5} = 6.02\,N + 1.76\ \text{dB}SQNR=20log10​LSB/12​2NLSB/(22​)​=20log10​(2N23​​)=N⋅20log10​2+20log10​1.5​=6.02N+1.76 dB

For N=12N = 12N=12 this is 74.0 dB; for N=16N = 16N=16 it is 98.1 dB. A real converter also has thermal noise and distortion, measured together as SINAD. Inverting the formula gives the effective number of bits, the resolution of an ideal ADC with the same SINAD:

ENOB=SINAD−1.76 dB6.02 dB\text{ENOB} = \frac{\text{SINAD} - 1.76\ \text{dB}}{6.02\ \text{dB}}ENOB=6.02 dBSINAD−1.76 dB​

With a shorted input you can measure only the noise standard deviation σ\sigmaσ. Putting SNR=(full-scale sine rms)/σ\text{SNR} = (\text{full-scale sine rms})/\sigmaSNR=(full-scale sine rms)/σ into the same formula gives a noise-only ENOB that can be computed from a DC capture:

ENOBnoise=N−log⁡2 ⁣(12  σLSB)\text{ENOB}_{\text{noise}} = N - \log_2\!\left(\sqrt{12}\;\frac{\sigma}{\text{LSB}}\right)ENOBnoise​=N−log2​(12​LSBσ​)

ESP32 native ADC. The Espressif documents checked for this README give no ENOB or SNR for the C3 or S3 ADC. What they do give:

  • DNL ±7\pm 7±7 LSB and INL ±12\pm 12±12 LSB for the ESP32-C3 (Espressif 2025 comparison article).
  • DNL ±4\pm 4±4 LSB and INL ±8\pm 8±8 LSB for the ESP32-S3 (same article).
  • A total error of ±35 mV\pm 35\,\text{mV}±35mV on the C3's 0 to 2500 mV range (C3 datasheet table, as reproduced on the Espressif forum).

A DNL larger than 1 LSB means some codes are missing or doubled, so resolution is already below 12 bits before noise is counted. One third-party blog test of an original ESP32 (a different chip, and not independently checked for this README) reported σ≈16\sigma \approx 16σ≈16 LSB, which by the formula above is 6.2 bits. For comparison, σ\sigmaσ = 1, 2 or 4 LSB would give 10.2, 9.2 or 8.2 bits.

The real ENOB of this board's ADC must be measured. In the current sketch, CAL ZERO reads 2048 shorted-input samples per channel and prints their peak-to-peak spread. For 2048 Gaussian samples the expected spread is about 6.9σ6.9\sigma6.9σ (Monte Carlo), so σ≈p-p/6.9\sigma \approx \text{p-p}/6.9σ≈p-p/6.9. This is a rough estimate, since one interference spike inflates it. Accumulating the sum of squares and printing σ\sigmaσ directly would be better.

T3.3 Input-referred resolution of each path

What matters to the user is the step size and noise at the probe. So every ADC-side quantity is divided by the gain between VinV_{\text{in}}Vin​ and the ADC pin.

V2 direct. The level shifter has gain 1 from VinV_{\text{in}}Vin​ to VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​, so the input-referred LSB equals the ADC LSB: 805.7 µV nominal (1 mV as reported).

V1 auto-range. Gain stage bbb multiplies the input by GbG_bGb​ before the ADC, so one ADC code corresponds to a smaller input change:

LSBin,b=LSBADCGb,ΔNb=log⁡2Gb\text{LSB}_{\text{in},b} = \frac{\text{LSB}_{\text{ADC}}}{G_b},\qquad \Delta N_b = \log_2 G_bLSBin,b​=Gb​LSBADC​​,ΔNb​=log2​Gb​
  • Stage 1: 805.7/5.5=146.5 μV805.7/5.5 = 146.5\,\mu\text{V}805.7/5.5=146.5μV (181.8 µV with 1 mV rounding), a gain of log⁡25.5=+2.46\log_2 5.5 = +2.46log2​5.5=+2.46 bits.
  • Stage 2: 805.7/2.36=341.4 μV805.7/2.36 = 341.4\,\mu\text{V}805.7/2.36=341.4μV (423.7 µV with 1 mV rounding), a gain of log⁡22.36=+1.24\log_2 2.36 = +1.24log2​2.36=+1.24 bits.

The catch is that gain cannot separate signal from noise that is already on VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​. Referring all the noise of stage bbb to the probe:

σin,b2=σls,b2+σstage,b2+σADC2+LSBADC2/12Gb2\sigma_{\text{in},b}^2 = \sigma_{\text{ls},b}^2 + \frac{\sigma_{\text{stage},b}^2 + \sigma_{\text{ADC}}^2 + \text{LSB}_{\text{ADC}}^2/12}{G_b^2}σin,b2​=σls,b2​+Gb2​σstage,b2​+σADC2​+LSBADC2​/12​

Only the terms that enter after the gain shrink by GbG_bGb​: the stage's own resistor and op-amp noise (referred to its output), the ADC noise and quantization. The level-shifter noise σls,b\sigma_{\text{ls},b}σls,b​ (the part that fits inside stage bbb's bandwidth) is not divided by GbG_bGb​.

Stage 1 only helps if it is driven. In the schematic as drawn, a signal inside window 1 is also inside window 2, so the mux selects channel 3 (Y3, not connected) and stage 1 is never selected. The firmware then falls back to the direct path, and stage 2 is driven only for 0.275 V<∣Vin∣<0.70 V0.275\,\text{V} < |V_{\text{in}}| < 0.70\,\text{V}0.275V<∣Vin​∣<0.70V (design-intent windows). The PCB shows extra resistors (R28 to R38) that may change this, so check the built board. All stage-1 numbers below assume the stage is driven.

V3 ADS8681. LSB = 5.12 V/65536=78.125 μV5.12\,\text{V}/65536 = 78.125\,\mu\text{V}5.12V/65536=78.125μV and σq=22.55 μV\sigma_q = 22.55\,\mu\text{V}σq​=22.55μV. TI's datasheet table, as returned by searches (TI's PDF could not be opened for this review), gives these values for the ±0.625 VREF\pm 0.625\,V_{\text{REF}}±0.625VREF​ range: SNR about 90 dB typical (87.75 dB minimum) and SINAD 90 dB typical (87.65 dB minimum). Typical values are at 25 °C with AVDD = 5 V and the internal 4.096 V reference; minima cover −40 to +125 °C. The headline 92 dB SNR belongs to the ±3 VREF\pm 3\,V_{\text{REF}}±3VREF​ range. Confirm these in the electrical-characteristics table, and note that the ADS8681W variant is much noisier (about 77 dB SNR on this range).

  • ENOB: 90 dB gives 14.66 bits (14.27 bits at the minimum).
  • SINAD vs SNR: distortion is far lower (TI's product page quotes THD of −107 dB), so SINAD ≈ SNR here.
  • Input-referred noise: 90 dB below a full-scale sine (2.56/2=1.810 Vrms2.56/\sqrt{2} = 1.810\,\text{V}_{\text{rms}}2.56/2​=1.810Vrms​) is 1.810 V×10−90/20=57.2 μVrms1.810\,\text{V}\times 10^{-90/20} = 57.2\,\mu\text{V}_{\text{rms}}1.810V×10−90/20=57.2μVrms​, about 0.73 LSB. Quantization accounts for 22.6 µV of this and the converter's analog noise for the remaining 52.6 µV.
  • Unused range: the probe swing of ±1.65 V\pm 1.65\,\text{V}±1.65V uses only part of the ±2.56 V\pm 2.56\,\text{V}±2.56V range. That costs log⁡2(2.56/1.65)=0.63\log_2(2.56/1.65) = 0.63log2​(2.56/1.65)=0.63 bits (3.8 dB). The noise stays at 57 µV, so a ±1.65 V\pm 1.65\,\text{V}±1.65V sine gets 86.2 dB, about 14.0 effective bits.

T3.4 Thermal noise of resistors and op-amps

Every resistor generates Johnson-Nyquist noise from the random motion of electrons. Its density is flat with frequency, so the RMS value grows with the square root of the bandwidth BBB that reaches the ADC:

vn=4kTRB,eR=4kTR  [V/Hz]v_n = \sqrt{4kTRB},\qquad e_R = \sqrt{4kTR}\ \ \left[\text{V}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}\right]vn​=4kTRB​,eR​=4kTR​  [V/Hz​]

Here TTT is absolute temperature, not the sample period. At T=300 KT = 300\,\text{K}T=300K, 10 kΩ gives 12.87 nV/√Hz and 20 kΩ gives 18.20 nV/√Hz (5 kΩ: 9.10; 255 kΩ: 65.0). Real filters do not cut off like a brick wall, so BBB is the equivalent noise bandwidth: the width of a brick-wall filter that passes the same noise power.

Bn=∫0∞∣H(f)∣2 df={π2 f−3dB≈1.57 f−3dBsingle poleπ22 f−3dB≈1.11 f−3dB2nd-order Butterworthπ4 fp≈1.22 f−3dBtwo equal real poles at fpB_n = \int_0^{\infty} |H(f)|^2\,df = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\pi}{2}\,f_{-3\text{dB}} \approx 1.57\,f_{-3\text{dB}} & \text{single pole}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\,f_{-3\text{dB}} \approx 1.11\,f_{-3\text{dB}} & \text{2nd-order Butterworth}\\ \dfrac{\pi}{4}\,f_p \approx 1.22\,f_{-3\text{dB}} & \text{two equal real poles at } f_p \end{cases}Bn​=∫0∞​∣H(f)∣2df=⎩⎨⎧​2π​f−3dB​≈1.57f−3dB​22​π​f−3dB​≈1.11f−3dB​4π​fp​≈1.22f−3dB​​single pole2nd-order Butterworthtwo equal real poles at fp​​

The bandwidth is what makes the two halves of this board so different:

  • ADS8681 path. Its internal 2nd-order anti-aliasing filter has f−3dB≈15 kHzf_{-3\text{dB}} \approx 15\,\text{kHz}f−3dB​≈15kHz on every range (TI datasheet, typical). With the two-real-pole model of T1.5 (fpf_pfp​ = 23.3 kHz), Bn=18.3 kHzB_n = 18.3\,\text{kHz}Bn​=18.3kHz. A 10 kΩ resistor in this band gives 1.74 µV. The resistor noise that actually reaches AIN_P is that of Rs ∥ (R3+R6) ∥ RINR_s \,\|\, (R_3 + R_6) \,\|\, R_{\text{IN}}Rs​∥(R3​+R6​)∥RIN​, where RsR_sRs​ is the source resistance, R3+R6=20 kΩR_3 + R_6 = 20\,\text{k}\OmegaR3​+R6​=20kΩ and RIN≈1 MΩR_{\text{IN}} \approx 1\,\text{M}\OmegaRIN​≈1MΩ. That is 0.12 µV for a 50 Ω source, 0.54 µV for 1 kΩ, and at most 2.44 µV with the input open. All are negligible next to the converter's 57 µV.
  • Level shifter (IC1 section 2). Noise gain 2 with GBW = 50 MHz gives a closed-loop bandwidth of about 25 MHz, so Bn=39.3 MHzB_n = 39.3\,\text{MHz}Bn​=39.3MHz. In this band a single 10 kΩ resistor already gives 80.7 µV.

With the probe driven by a low-impedance source (or shorted, as in CAL ZERO), the level-shifter output noise density is the power sum of four terms:

  • the 5 kΩ Thevenin resistance of R3 ∥ R6 at the non-inverting input, times the noise gain of 2;
  • the feedback pair R4 ∥ R5 (also 5 kΩ), times 2;
  • the op-amp voltage noise, times 2;
  • the noise of the buffered Vref1V_{\text{ref1}}Vref1​, times 1.

The TSV794 voltage noise is 6.5 nV/√Hz typical at 10 kHz (ST datasheet). It is assumed flat up to the closed-loop bandwidth, which the datasheet figures found for this review do not confirm. Current noise is neglected (CMOS inputs, pA bias). The R1/R2 divider (5 kΩ Thevenin, no filter capacitor assumed) plus the buffer give eref1=9.102+6.52=11.2 nV/Hze_{\text{ref1}} = \sqrt{9.10^2 + 6.5^2} = 11.2\,\text{nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}eref1​=9.102+6.52​=11.2nV/Hz​.

Assumptions behind the table:

  • Rin+RonR_{\text{in}} + R_{\text{on}}Rin​+Ron​ is chosen to give the design gains with RfR_fRf​ = 255 kΩ. Only R7 is documented. Because the sum is fixed by the gain, the split between RinR_{\text{in}}Rin​ and RonR_{\text{on}}Ron​ (unspecified for the CD4052B at 3.3 V) does not change the noise. RonR_{\text{on}}Ron​ does vary with signal level, which makes the gain slightly signal-dependent. CAL BANDS' straight-line fit cannot remove that.
  • The upstream term is integrated through both the level-shifter pole and the stage pole.
  • The op-amp is modelled as a single pole. In reality a few pF of op-amp and mux input capacitance against 255 kΩ raises the high-frequency noise gain and can cause peaking. A small capacitor across RfR_fRf​ would both stabilise the stage and narrow its noise bandwidth.

Three lessons follow:

  • Largest term. At the stage-1 output the largest single term is the amplified level-shifter noise (170 nV/√Hz). Within the stage's own noise, RfR_fRf​ and RinR_{\text{in}}Rin​ supply 166 of the 181 nV/√Hz, so scaling all stage resistors down by 10 would cut those two terms by 10=3.2\sqrt{10} = 3.210​=3.2.
  • Stage 1 vs direct. Stage 1 is only a little quieter than the direct path at the probe (148 µV versus 194 µV). That is mostly because its 7.7 MHz bandwidth filters the level-shifter noise (194 µV down to 94 µV), not because of its gain.
  • Stage 2 vs direct. Stage 2 is noisier than the direct path at the probe (282 µV), because its own noise referred to the probe (256 µV) outweighs that filtering. The gain stages only pay off once the ESP32 ADC's own noise dominates (see the budget).

T3.5 Aliasing of wideband noise

A sample-and-hold takes an instantaneous snapshot. The variance of each sample is therefore the noise power integrated over the whole front-end bandwidth, whatever fsf_sfs​ is. Noise above fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 does not disappear; it folds into the band from 0 to fs/2f_s/2fs​/2:

σsample2=∫0∞e2 ∣H(f)∣2 df=e2Bn(independent of fs),σsampleσin-band=Bnfs/2\sigma_{\text{sample}}^2 = \int_0^{\infty} e^2\,|H(f)|^2\,df = e^2 B_n \quad\text{(independent of } f_s\text{)}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_{\text{sample}}}{\sigma_{\text{in-band}}} = \sqrt{\frac{B_n}{f_s/2}}σsample2​=∫0∞​e2∣H(f)∣2df=e2Bn​(independent of fs​),σin-band​σsample​​=fs​/2Bn​​​

At fs=10 kS/sf_s = 10\,\text{kS/s}fs​=10kS/s, the level shifter's noise inside 0 to 5 kHz is only 30.9 nV×5000=2.19 μV30.9\,\text{nV}\times\sqrt{5000} = 2.19\,\mu\text{V}30.9nV×5000​=2.19μV. Yet each sample carries the full 194 µV: a factor of 88.6, or 39 dB. There is no RC filter in front of the ESP32 ADC pins, so the op-amps set the bandwidth. The ESP32's own sampling bandwidth is undocumented and is assumed to be wider.

As an illustration of a possible change, sized for the default 10 kS/s: put 100 Ω in series with 100 nF to GND at each ADC pin (f−3dB=15.9 kHzf_{-3\text{dB}} = 15.9\,\text{kHz}f−3dB​=15.9kHz, Bn=25 kHzB_n = 25\,\text{kHz}Bn​=25kHz). The series resistor matters because the TSV79x is rated stable with only about 1 nF of direct capacitive load (typical, ST). The 100 nF matches Espressif's recommendation for the ADC pad, and it is large enough to swamp the SAR's charge kickback when the ADC switches between pins (T2.4).

  • The direct-path noise would drop to 4.9 µV.
  • Stage 1 would drop to 39 µV at the pin (7.1 µV at the probe), and stage 2 to 23 µV (9.7 µV).
  • The resistor itself adds only 1.3 nV/√Hz, and the kT/C noise of 100 nF is 0.20 µV.
  • When the ADC switches to this pin from one up to 3 V away, its sampling capacitor (assumed 5 pF) disturbs the 100 nF by about 0.15 mV. With 1 kΩ and 10 nF (the same corner) it would be 1.5 mV, about 2 LSB.

Its corner is above fs/2=5 kHzf_s/2 = 5\,\text{kHz}fs​/2=5kHz, so it mainly limits noise. A filter that also stops signals above fs/2f_s/2fs​/2 from aliasing needs a lower corner and a steeper roll-off. The ADS8681 path already has its 15 kHz filter inside the chip.

T3.6 kT/C noise of the sampling capacitor

When the sampling switch opens, the thermal noise of its on-resistance is frozen on the hold capacitor. Integrating 4kTR4kTR4kTR through the single-pole RC, with Bn=(π/2)⋅1/(2πRC)B_n = (\pi/2)\cdot 1/(2\pi RC)Bn​=(π/2)⋅1/(2πRC), makes RRR cancel:

vn2‾=4kTR⋅π2⋅12πRC=kTC,vn=kTC\overline{v_n^2} = 4kTR\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi RC} = \frac{kT}{C},\qquad v_n = \sqrt{\frac{kT}{C}}vn2​​=4kTR⋅2π​⋅2πRC1​=CkT​,vn​=CkT​​

At 300 K, 1 pF gives 64.4 µV, 2 pF gives 45.5 µV and 5 pF gives 28.8 µV. The ESP32 hold capacitance is not documented. For a few pF this is under 0.1 LSB of the native ADC, so it is negligible. The ADS8681's internal sampling capacitor sits behind its PGA and filter, and its kT/C noise is already included in the datasheet SNR.

T3.7 Reference and supply noise

Vref1V_{\text{ref1}}Vref1​ is half of VDD, so the level-shifted node is Vls=Vin+VDD/2V_{\text{ls}} = V_{\text{in}} + V_{DD}/2Vls​=Vin​+VDD​/2. The ESP32 ADC measures against its own internal reference, not against VDD, so the measurement is not ratiometric. Half of any supply ripple δVDD\delta V_{DD}δVDD​ therefore appears in the direct-path reading as if it were input signal. With an assumed 10 mV p-p ripple on the XIAO's 3.3 V rail, that is 5 mV p-p, about 6.2 nominal LSB. A 1 % DC change of VDD shifts VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​ by 16.5 mV. CAL ZERO removes the offset present at calibration time, but not later drift.

The gain stages behave better because both their references come from VDD. Write Vref1=VDD2(1+ε1)V_{\text{ref1}} = \tfrac{V_{DD}}{2}(1+\varepsilon_1)Vref1​=2VDD​​(1+ε1​) for the R1/R2 divider and Vref2=VDD2(1+ε2)V_{\text{ref2}} = \tfrac{V_{DD}}{2}(1+\varepsilon_2)Vref2​=2VDD​​(1+ε2​) for the R24/R27 divider. Ripple. With equal dividers the VDD/2 terms collapse to VDD/2, so the ripple at the stage output is δVDD/2\delta V_{DD}/2δVDD​/2. It is not multiplied by GbG_bGb​. Referred to the probe it is divided by GbG_bGb​: δVDD/11\delta V_{DD}/11δVDD​/11 for stage 1 and δVDD/4.72\delta V_{DD}/4.72δVDD​/4.72 for stage 2.
