ADS8681 path. The ADS8681 uses its internal 4.096 V reference with AIN_GND = GND, so it does not depend on VDD with one exception. The probe's source resistance RsR_sRs​ forms a divider with the 20 kΩ load to Vref1V_{\text{ref1}}Vref1​, so a fraction Rs/(2(Rs+20 kΩ))R_s/\big(2(R_s + 20\,\text{k}\Omega)\big)Rs​/(2(Rs​+20kΩ)) of δVDD\delta V_{DD}δVDD​ reaches AIN_P (the same happens on the native paths). That is 0.12 % for a 50 Ω source and 2.4 % for 1 kΩ. Ripple on its AVDD (USB 5 V) is set by the ADS8681's supply rejection, which is not analysed here.

The window-comparator thresholds also track VDD: window 1 sits at Vin=±VDD/12=±0.275 VV_{\text{in}} = \pm V_{DD}/12 = \pm 0.275\,\text{V}Vin​=±VDD​/12=±0.275V, so a 1 % VDD change moves each edge by 2.75 mV. These hardware edges decide which mux channel, and so which stage, is driven. The firmware's software windows only decide which stage to try, and its consistency test rejects a stage that is not driven. So a small shift costs some band-switching range, not accuracy.

T3.8 Comparator hysteresis versus noise

A comparator whose input sits near its threshold will chatter if noise carries the input back and forth across it. Positive feedback fixes this by moving the threshold away from the input once the output has switched.

For comparator A, R30 = 1 MΩ feeds OUTA back to the non-inverting input, which sees the ladder through R11. The source resistance is R11 plus the ladder's Thevenin resistance at the upper tap (topology-derived):

Rs=R11+R19 ∥ (R20+R21)=2.0 kΩ+5 kΩ ∥ 7 kΩ=4.92 kΩ,ΔVhyst=VDD RsRs+R30=3.3 V×4.92 kΩ1004.9 kΩ=16.1 mVR_s = R_{11} + R_{19}\,\|\,(R_{20}+R_{21}) = 2.0\,\text{k}\Omega + 5\,\text{k}\Omega\,\|\,7\,\text{k}\Omega = 4.92\,\text{k}\Omega, \qquad \Delta V_{\text{hyst}} = V_{DD}\,\frac{R_s}{R_s + R_{30}} = 3.3\,\text{V}\times\frac{4.92\,\text{k}\Omega}{1004.9\,\text{k}\Omega} = 16.1\,\text{mV}Rs​=R11​+R19​∥(R20​+R21​)=2.0kΩ+5kΩ∥7kΩ=4.92kΩ,ΔVhyst​=VDD​Rs​+R30​Rs​​=3.3V×1004.9kΩ4.92kΩ​=16.1mV

The trip point is VthR30/(Rs+R30)+VOUTRs/(Rs+R30)V_{\text{th}}R_{30}/(R_s+R_{30}) + V_{\text{OUT}}R_s/(R_s+R_{30})Vth​R30​/(Rs​+R30​)+VOUT​Rs​/(Rs​+R30​). It is 1.9317 V while OUTA is high and 1.9156 V while OUTA is low, around the nominal 1.925 V. The MCP6544 adds internal hysteresis of 3.3 mV typical (Microchip MCP6541 family). Distributor listings also show 6.5 mV, which appears to be the maximum; the guaranteed minimum is below 3.3 mV. Comparator A's total is therefore about 19.4 mV typical.

Comparator B's 1 MΩ feedback (R31), and that of window 2's comparator C, lands on the Input node instead. That node is driven by the level-shifter output, whose impedance is assumed to be of the order of 1 Ω. The feedback therefore adds only about 3.3 V×1 Ω/1 MΩ=3.3 μV3.3\,\text{V}\times 1\,\Omega/1\,\text{M}\Omega = 3.3\,\mu\text{V}3.3V×1Ω/1MΩ=3.3μV, so B and C rely on the internal 3.3 mV (typical) alone. Window 2's comparator D cannot be computed because R15 to R17 are undocumented. If it mirrors A (R14 = 2 kΩ isolation, R12 or R13 = 1 MΩ feedback), a ladder Thevenin resistance of 2 to 3 kΩ would give 13 to 16 mV.

For Gaussian noise, 99.9 % of samples lie within ±3.29σ\pm 3.29\sigma±3.29σ, a peak-to-peak band of about 6.6σ6.6\sigma6.6σ. A rule of thumb is that hysteresis must be wider than this:

ΔVhyst>6.6 σ⇒σmax⁡=ΔVhyst6.6\Delta V_{\text{hyst}} > 6.6\,\sigma \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \sigma_{\max} = \frac{\Delta V_{\text{hyst}}}{6.6}ΔVhyst​>6.6σ⇒σmax​=6.6ΔVhyst​​

Here is how the board compares with this rule:

  • Board noise. Comparator A tolerates up to about 3 mV rms of noise (2.45 mV from the external hysteresis alone), but B and C tolerate only 0.50 mV rms. The board's own level-shifter noise (194 µV rms, 1.3 mV p-p over 25 MHz) is below both. The comparators also respond far more slowly than that bandwidth (about 4 µs propagation delay), so they see less of it.
  • Probe noise. A probe signal carrying more than about 0.5 mV rms of its own noise will make B and C chatter near their thresholds, and the AND gates and the mux then toggle. The firmware's consistency test (each stage must agree within 0.04 V with the direct reading interpolated to its read slot, T4.5) rejects samples taken mid-switch and falls back to the direct reading, so the expected effect is mostly a flickering band code rather than a wrong voltage.
  • Comparator offset. The MCP6544's input offset (up to about ±7 mV in distributor listings) is larger than B and C's hysteresis. It moves the thresholds but does not cause chatter.

The same rule applies to the firmware trigger, which arms below L−hL - hL−h and fires at LLL on the selected trigger channel, with h=0.03 Vh = 0.03\,\text{V}h=0.03V by default. It stays clean for noise up to 30/6.6=4.6 mV30/6.6 = 4.6\,\text{mV}30/6.6=4.6mV rms on that channel. On the direct path that holds in the optimistic case below (1.65 mV) but not in the pessimistic one (12.9 mV rms, about 85 mV p-p), where hhh would have to be raised or the trigger run on a short moving average.

T3.9 Averaging and oversampling

Averaging MMM samples whose noise is uncorrelated keeps the signal and shrinks the noise standard deviation by M\sqrt{M}M​. (MMM is used here because NNN already means bits.)

σvˉ=σM,ΔSNR=10log⁡10M dB,ΔNeff=12log⁡2M\sigma_{\bar v} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{M}},\qquad \Delta\text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}M\ \text{dB},\qquad \Delta N_{\text{eff}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 Mσvˉ​=M​σ​,ΔSNR=10log10​M dB,ΔNeff​=21​log2​M

MMM = 4, 16 and 256 give 6.0, 12.0 and 24.1 dB, i.e. 1, 2 and 4 extra bits. CAL ZERO's 2048-sample mean is 33.1 dB (a factor of 45) quieter than a single sample for the white part of the noise. The 2048 reads take only about 20 to 40 ms, so 1/f noise, drift and mains hum are not averaged away to the same degree.

Oversampling and decimation apply the same idea in time. You sample at OSR⋅fs\text{OSR}\cdot f_sOSR⋅fs​, low-pass filter, keep every OSR-th value, and gain half a bit per doubling of OSR. One native read takes 10 to 20 µs (50 to 100 kS/s), so at best, decimating 100 kS/s to 10 kS/s (OSR = 10) would give +10 dB, about 1.7 bits. Three conditions apply:

  • The noise must be at least about 0.5 LSB rms so that it acts as dither. This is expected for the ESP32 (to be confirmed by measurement), and it is also what lets averaging see through the 1 mV rounding of analogReadMilliVolts().
  • The noise must be uncorrelated between samples. Supply ripple and interference are not.
  • Averaging cannot remove deterministic errors, such as the ESP32's INL of up to ±12\pm 12±12 LSB.

For repetitive signals, averaging successive triggered frames gives the same M\sqrt{M}M​ gain without lowering the bandwidth, but only up to the trigger's timing jitter. The trigger is tested only at sample instants, so each frame is misaligned by a random fraction of one sample period (T/12=28.9 μsT/\sqrt{12} = 28.9\,\mu\text{s}T/12​=28.9μs rms at 10 kS/s). Averaging then acts as a low-pass filter ∣sin⁡(πfT)/(πfT)∣|\sin(\pi fT)/(\pi fT)|∣sin(πfT)/(πfT)∣, which is −3 dB at 0.44 fs0.44\,f_s0.44fs​ and −3.9 dB at fs/2f_s/2fs​/2. Noise adds a further jitter σt=σv/∣dv/dt∣\sigma_t = \sigma_v/|dv/dt|σt​=σv​/∣dv/dt∣ at the crossing. For example, 1.65 mV of noise on a 1 V, 100 Hz sine gives 2.6 µs, much smaller than the sample-grid term.

Choosing the averaging window to reject mains hum. Averaging is also a filter. The mean of nnn samples spaced TTT apart passes a tone of frequency fff with gain

∣Havg(f)∣=∣sin⁡(πfnT)n sin⁡(πfT)∣≈∣sin⁡(πfTw)πfTw∣,Tw=nT|H_\text{avg}(f)| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi f nT)}{n\,\sin(\pi f T)}\right| \approx \left|\frac{\sin(\pi f T_w)}{\pi f T_w}\right|, \qquad T_w = nT∣Havg​(f)∣=​nsin(πfT)sin(πfnT)​​≈​πfTw​sin(πfTw​)​​,Tw​=nT

Its nulls sit at multiples of 1/Tw1/T_w1/Tw​. A 100 ms window holds exactly 5 cycles of 50 Hz and 6 cycles of 60 Hz, so it nulls both mains frequencies and all their harmonics. The default record (1000 samples at 10 kS/s) is exactly such a window, so the host's mean rejects hum. If the real sample rate is off by 1 %, about 1 % of the hum (−40 dB) gets through.

CAL ZERO's 2048 reads are not paced, so its window is however long 2048 reads take: about 20 to 41 ms on the native paths, and roughly 15 ms on the ADS8681, whose reads are faster. The worst-case hum left in the mean is ∣Havg∣|H_\text{avg}|∣Havg​∣ times the hum amplitude:

Window 50 Hz residual 60 Hz residual
15 ms (ADS8681) 30 % 11 %
20 ms 0 16 %
30 ms 21 % 10 %
41 ms 2.4 % 13 %
100 ms 0 0

For example, 1 mV of hum picked up by the shorting lead could leave up to 0.21 mV in a native mid-point (about a quarter of an ESP32 LSB) and up to 0.3 mV in the ADS8681's (about 4 of its LSBs). Pacing CAL ZERO so that its 2048 samples span exactly 100 ms (20.48 kS/s) would null both mains frequencies on every path.

What the budget shows:

Dividing that noise by GbG_bGb​ is therefore the real benefit of the V1 gain stages, more than the nominal extra bits. If the ADC turns out to be quiet, stage 2's advantage nearly disappears, because its own analog noise (282 µV) already exceeds the direct path's (194 µV).
  • Analog front end: its noise is set mainly by the level shifter, the high-value stage resistors and the missing anti-aliasing filter, which lets tens of MHz of noise bandwidth alias into every sample.
  • ADS8681: this path is about 30 to 230 times quieter than the direct path, and 6 to 40 times quieter than stage 1. It has both a better converter and a 15 kHz filter that limits the noise bandwidth.

T3.11 Comparing the three paths: SNR versus signal size

Take a sine of amplitude AAA on a path whose input-referred noise is σin\sigma_\text{in}σin​ (the last rows of the budget table). Its signal-to-noise ratio, and the equivalent number of bits, are

SNR(A)=20log⁡10A/2σin,ENOB(A)=SNR(A)−1.766.02\text{SNR}(A) = 20\log_{10}\frac{A/\sqrt{2}}{\sigma_\text{in}}, \qquad \text{ENOB}(A) = \frac{\text{SNR}(A) - 1.76}{6.02}SNR(A)=20log10​σin​A/2​​,ENOB(A)=6.02SNR(A)−1.76​

Each path only carries signals up to its usable range (T1.4; ESP32-S3 linear range 0.10-3.00 V, smaller on a C3). Below, σADC\sigma_\text{ADC}σADC​ is 2 LSB / 16 LSB, as in the budget:

V2 direct 1.35 V 55.2 dB / 37.4 dB 32.6 dB / 14.8 dB

Two results stand out:

  • A gain stage does not widen its own path's dynamic range. When the ESP32's noise dominates, a stage shrinks both the input range and the input-referred noise by GbG_bGb​, so every native path reaches the same SNR at full range (37.4 dB in the pessimistic case). Auto-ranging pays off in combined dynamic range: the largest signal the direct path can carry, over the noise floor of the highest-gain stage. That is 69.2 dB (optimistic) or 52.2 dB (pessimistic), 14.0 to 14.8 dB more than the direct path and close to 20log⁡10G1=14.820\log_{10}G_1 = 14.820log10​G1​=14.8 dB. With stage 1 undriven, as drawn (T4.4), stage 2 sets the floor and the figures fall to 62.1 dB and 44.8 dB.
DRAUTO=20log⁡10Amax⁡,direct/2σin,1\text{DR}_\text{AUTO} = 20\log_{10}\frac{A_{\max,\text{direct}}/\sqrt{2}}{\sigma_{\text{in},1}}DRAUTO​=20log10​σin,1​Amax,direct​/2​​
  • The ADS8681 wins at every amplitude. At any given amplitude it is 29 to 47 dB ahead of the direct path, and its 86.2 dB dynamic range is still 17 to 34 dB more than the auto-ranged combination. That is the quantitative answer to the question the board was built to ask.

T4. The math inside the firmware and the measurements

The firmware and the Python host apply a short chain of algebra to every reading. They undo the analog front end to get probe volts back, decide which acquisition path to trust, line the samples up in time, and turn a record into readable numbers. This section derives each step from the schematic and plugs in this board's values. Every number here is a design or theory value, computed from the schematic, datasheets or a labelled assumption. None of them is a bench measurement.

T4.1 Reconstruction: from ADC reading back to probe volts

Direct path (V2, pin D2). Section 2 of IC1 is a non-inverting summing amplifier. R3 and R6 (10 kΩ each) average the probe and the 1.65 V reference at its non-inverting input, and R4/R5 give a gain of 2. The halving and the doubling cancel, so the probe is simply shifted up by VrefV_{\text{ref}}Vref​:

V+=Vin+Vref2,Vls=(1+R4R5)V+=Vin+VrefV_+ = \frac{V_{\text{in}} + V_{\text{ref}}}{2}, \qquad V_{\text{ls}} = \left(1 + \frac{R_4}{R_5}\right) V_+ = V_{\text{in}} + V_{\text{ref}}V+​=2Vin​+Vref​​,Vls​=(1+R5​R4​​)V+​=Vin​+Vref​

Real resistors and a real reference are slightly off. The firmware therefore models the reading as a general straight line, VD2=mid+g VinV_{D2} = \text{mid} + g\,V_{\text{in}}VD2​=mid+gVin​, and inverts it with calibrated constants (defaults mid = 1.65 V, g = 1.0):

Vin=VD2−middirectgdirectV_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{D2} - \text{mid}_{\text{direct}}}{g_{\text{direct}}}Vin​=gdirect​VD2​−middirect​​

On this path the ESP32 ADC sets the limit, not the op-amp. If the ADC is trusted from 0.10 V to 3.00 V (the span the firmware uses as "linear" for the gain stages), the probe range is −1.55 V to +1.35 V. The ESP32-C3 is specified only up to about 2.5 V at its highest attenuation, which lowers the top end to about +0.85 V. analogReadMilliVolts() returns whole millivolts, and the raw 12-bit code step at this attenuation is somewhat finer (roughly range / 4096, about 0.6–0.8 mV), so the integer-millivolt output sets a 1 mV step at the probe.

All the reconstructions return the voltage at RawInput itself. RawInput is loaded by R3 + R6 = 20 kΩ to the 1.65 V buffer (in parallel with the ADS8681's ≥ 1 MΩ to GND), so a source with internal resistance is pulled toward 1.65 V. For example, a 0 V source with 1 kΩ of internal resistance sits at about +80 mV. Calibrating with a stiff (low-impedance) source does not remove this.

External ADC (V3, ADS8681). AIN_P is wired to RawInput itself, so there is no level shift to undo. Range code 0x4 selects ±0.625·VREF = ±2.56 V with straight-binary output, so 0 V reads as code 0x8000. With N=16N = 16N=16, the ideal transfer function the firmware assumes, and its inverse, are:

LSB=2×2.56 V216=78.125 μV,code=⌊Vin+2.56 VLSB⌋,Vads=−2.56 V+code⋅LSB\text{LSB} = \frac{2 \times 2.56\,\text{V}}{2^{16}} = 78.125\,\mu\text{V}, \qquad \text{code} = \left\lfloor \frac{V_{\text{in}} + 2.56\,\text{V}}{\text{LSB}} \right\rfloor, \qquad V_{\text{ads}} = -2.56\,\text{V} + \text{code}\cdot\text{LSB}LSB=2162×2.56V​=78.125μV,code=⌊LSBVin​+2.56V​⌋,Vads​=−2.56V+code⋅LSB

The firmware then applies Vin=(Vads−midext)/gextV_{\text{in}} = (V_{\text{ads}} - \text{mid}_{\text{ext}})/g_{\text{ext}}Vin​=(Vads​−midext​)/gext​, with defaults 0 V and 1.0. The probe's ±1.65 V maps to codes 11 648 through 53 888. That is 42 240 codes, or about 15.4 of the 16 bits. ±2.56 V is the ADS8681's narrowest bipolar range, so no better fit is available. With the floor quantizer, the inverse returns the bottom edge of each code bin, which is a −LSB/2 = −39 µV bias. If the real converter puts its first transition half an LSB up (check the transfer-function figure in the datasheet), there is no bias. Either way, CAL ZERO absorbs it into mid_ext.

Gain stages (V1, pins D0 and D1). Each stage is an inverting amplifier biased at Vref2V_{\text{ref2}}Vref2​, the unbuffered R24/R27 divider. When its mux channel is on, the stage sees VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​ through Rin+RonR_{\text{in}} + R_{\text{on}}Rin​+Ron​, where RonR_{\text{on}}Ron​ is the CD4052B switch resistance. Writing the output in terms of the probe voltage separates an offset from a negative gain:

Vout=Vref2−G (Vls−Vref2)=Vref2−G (Vref−Vref2)⏟off+(−G)⏟g Vin,G=RfRin+RonV_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{ref2}} - G\,(V_{\text{ls}} - V_{\text{ref2}}) = \underbrace{V_{\text{ref2}} - G\,(V_{\text{ref}} - V_{\text{ref2}})}_{\text{off}} + \underbrace{(-G)}_{g}\,V_{\text{in}}, \qquad G = \frac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}} + R_{\text{on}}}Vout​=Vref2​−G(Vls​−Vref2​)=offVref2​−G(Vref​−Vref2​)​​+g(−G)​​Vin​,G=Rin​+Ron​Rf​​

The firmware stores the gain with its sign, so the stage is inverted by the same formula as the other paths:

Vin=Vout−offbgb,g1=−5.5,  g2=−2.36,  off1=off2=1.65 V (defaults)V_{\text{in}} = \frac{V_{\text{out}} - \text{off}_b}{g_b}, \qquad g_1 = -5.5,\; g_2 = -2.36,\; \text{off}_1 = \text{off}_2 = 1.65\,\text{V}\ \text{(defaults)}Vin​=gb​Vout​−offb​​,g1​=−5.5,g2​=−2.36,off1​=off2​=1.65V (defaults)

Two effects make calibration necessary:

  • Reference mismatch. Suppose the two 1.65 V dividers (R1/R2 and R24/R27) use 1 % resistors that err in opposite directions (assumed tolerance). Then Vref−Vref2V_{\text{ref}} - V_{\text{ref2}}Vref​−Vref2​ can reach 33 mV, and stage 1 multiplies it into a 0.18 V shift of its output. Including the shift of Vref2V_{\text{ref2}}Vref2​ itself, the true offset differs from the 1.65 V default by up to 0.20 V, which is 36 mV at the probe. That is almost the whole 40 mV tolerance of the consistency test (T4.5), so the stages need CAL BANDS before AUTO mode can be trusted.
  • Switch resistance. With R7 = 255 kΩ and an inferred Rin1R_{\text{in1}}Rin1​ = 46.4 kΩ, the ideal gain is G1G_1G1​ = 5.496. The CD4052B datasheet gives an on-resistance of 470 Ω typical and 1050 Ω maximum at 25 °C, but only for VDD = 5 V. Those values would lower the gain to 5.44 or 5.37, which is 1.0–2.2 % low. The tables have no 3.3 V row. At 3.3 V the resistance is higher and depends more on the signal level, so 1–2 % is a lower bound. The signal dependence also leaves a nonlinearity that a straight-line calibration cannot remove. The CAL BANDS residual (T4.6) shows how large it is.

T4.2 Window thresholds from the resistor ladder

Window 1 is set by a three-resistor divider from VDD to GND. The comparators compare VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​ against its two tap voltages:

Vupper=VDD R20+R21R19+R20+R21=3.3 V⋅712=1.925 V,Vlower=VDD R21R19+R20+R21=3.3 V⋅512=1.375 VV_{\text{upper}} = V_{DD}\,\frac{R_{20} + R_{21}}{R_{19} + R_{20} + R_{21}} = 3.3\,\text{V}\cdot\frac{7}{12} = 1.925\,\text{V}, \qquad V_{\text{lower}} = V_{DD}\,\frac{R_{21}}{R_{19} + R_{20} + R_{21}} = 3.3\,\text{V}\cdot\frac{5}{12} = 1.375\,\text{V}Vupper​=VDD​R19​+R20​+R21​R20​+R21​​=3.3V⋅127​=1.925V,Vlower​=VDD​R19​+R20​+R21​R21​​=3.3V⋅125​=1.375V

Subtracting Vref=VDD/2V_{\text{ref}} = V_{DD}/2Vref​=VDD​/2 gives the half-width at the probe. Because R19=R21R_{19} = R_{21}R19​=R21​, the window is centred on mid-rail, which is also where VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​ sits for 0 V in. The centre at the probe therefore stays at 0 V whatever VDD is, and only the width scales with VDD. A 1 % error in VDD moves each edge by 2.75 mV.

± VDD R202 (R19+R20+R21)=± VDD12=±0.275 V at the probe\pm\,\frac{V_{DD}\,R_{20}}{2\,(R_{19} + R_{20} + R_{21})} = \pm\,\frac{V_{DD}}{12} = \pm 0.275\,\text{V at the probe}±2(R19​+R20​+R21​)VDD​R20​​=±12VDD​​=±0.275V at the probe

1 1.35–1.95 V ±0.30 V 1.375–1.925 V = ±0.275 V (R19/R20/R21 = 5k/2k/5k, the redone ladder)
2 0.95–2.35 V ±0.70 V R15–R17 not documented; the design needs R16/Rtot=1.40/3.3=0.424R_{16}/R_{\text{tot}} = 1.40/3.3 = 0.424R16​/Rtot​=1.40/3.3=0.424 with R15=R17R_{15} = R_{17}R15​=R17​

For illustration only (these are not the board's values), a 5.6k/8.2k/5.6k ladder would give ±0.697 V.

Comparator A has positive feedback. R30 (1 MΩ) runs from OUTA to the threshold node, which the ladder feeds through R11, so R30 sees the ladder's Thévenin resistance plus R11, Rs=R19∥(R20+R21)+R11=2.917+2.0=4.917 kΩR_s = R_{19}\parallel(R_{20}+R_{21}) + R_{11} = 2.917 + 2.0 = 4.917\,\text{k}\OmegaRs​=R19​∥(R20​+R21​)+R11​=2.917+2.0=4.917kΩ. When OUTA switches between the rails (push-pull output assumed to swing 0 to 3.3 V), the upper threshold moves by a fraction of that swing:

ΔVhyst=VDD RsRs+R30=3.3 V⋅4.917 kΩ1004.9 kΩ=16.1 mV\Delta V_{\text{hyst}} = V_{DD}\,\frac{R_s}{R_s + R_{30}} = 3.3\,\text{V}\cdot\frac{4.917\,\text{k}\Omega}{1004.9\,\text{k}\Omega} = 16.1\,\text{mV}ΔVhyst​=VDD​Rs​+R30​Rs​​=3.3V⋅1004.9kΩ4.917kΩ​=16.1mV

The upper edge is therefore 1.932 V for a rising input and 1.916 V for a falling one. The R30 current (about 1.4 µA while OUTA is high) also lifts the lower tap by 2.9 mV, to about 1.378 V. Comparator B's feedback resistor R31 drives a node held by a low-impedance op-amp output, so B gets essentially no external hysteresis. It keeps only the MCP6544's small internal hysteresis, a few millivolts (3.3 mV typical in the MCP6541-family datasheet).

Resistor tolerance matters more than hysteresis. With 1 % parts in R19–R21 and R1/R2 (assumed), the worst-case window-1 edge lands anywhere from 0.242 V to 0.308 V from zero. Add 6.7 mV of rising-edge hysteresis and a comparator offset of up to about 7 mV (datasheet maximum, to be verified for this suffix), and the outermost edge is 0.321 V. That just fits inside the firmware's 0.05 V search margin (0.275 + 0.05 = 0.325 V, T4.5). CAL BANDS then replaces the nominal edges with learned ones.

T4.3 Choosing the stage gains

Each stage gain was chosen so that the full width of its window just fills the 0–3.3 V supply span, which is the op-amp's output range:

G=3.3 Vwindow width:G1=3.30.60=5.5,G2=3.31.40=2.357≈2.36G = \frac{3.3\,\text{V}}{\text{window width}}: \qquad G_1 = \frac{3.3}{0.60} = 5.5, \qquad G_2 = \frac{3.3}{1.40} = 2.357 \approx 2.36G=window width3.3V​:G1​=0.603.3​=5.5,G2​=1.403.3​=2.357≈2.36

These gains were sized for the website's windows. The redone ±0.275 V window is only 0.55 V wide, which would allow G1=6.0G_1 = 6.0G1​=6.0. Keeping G1=5.5G_1 = 5.5G1​=5.5 leaves headroom: the swing is 5.5×0.275=1.51 V5.5 \times 0.275 = 1.51\,\text{V}5.5×0.275=1.51V either side of 1.65 V, or 0.14 V to 3.16 V at D0. At ±0.70 V, stage 2 swings from −0.002 V to 3.302 V and touches both rails at the window edges.

The ESP32 ADC does not span 0–3.3 V, so the stages clip in the ADC before they reach the rails. The stages invert, so negative inputs drive the outputs high. The bias of 1.65 V is closer to the top of the ADC range than to the bottom, so the upper limit is reached first. Within the firmware's linear window of 0.10–3.00 V, the stages at their ideal gains are usable over these ranges:

Stage Usable VinV_{\text{in}}Vin​ for a 0.10–3.00 V reading Negative limit on a C3 (firmware limit 2.45 V)
1 (G1=5.5G_1 = 5.5G1​=5.5) −0.245 V to +0.275 V (window edge; the ADC alone would allow +0.282 V) −0.145 V
2 (G2=2.36G_2 = 2.36G2​=2.36) −0.572 V to +0.657 V −0.339 V

Covering all of ±0.275 V inside 0.10–3.00 V would need G1≤1.35/0.275=4.9G_1 \le 1.35/0.275 = 4.9G1​≤1.35/0.275=4.9, or 2.9 under the C3's 2.45 V limit. Beyond these limits the firmware rejects the stage reading and falls through to the next path (T4.5).

Comparator A is high when Vls<1.925V_{\text{ls}} < 1.925Vls​<1.925 V and comparator B is high when Vls>1.375V_{\text{ls}} > 1.375Vls​>1.375 V, so ANDing them yields the window-1 flag directly. Window 2 is built the same way from C and D, and the two flags drive the mux select lines:

W1=A∧B,W2=C∧D,SA=W1,SB=W2,channel=2SB+SAW_1 = A \land B, \qquad W_2 = C \land D, \qquad S_A = W_1,\quad S_B = W_2, \qquad \text{channel} = 2S_B + S_AW1​=A∧B,W2​=C∧D,SA​=W1​,SB​=W2​,channel=2SB​+SA​

  1. Channel 1 requires SA=1S_A = 1SA​=1 and SB=0S_B = 0SB​=0, that is, W1∧¬W2=1W_1 \land \lnot W_2 = 1W1​∧¬W2​=1.

Any VlsV_{\text{ls}}Vls​ inside window 1 is therefore also inside window 2, so W1⇒W2W_1 \Rightarrow W_2W1​⇒W2​, which is the same statement as W1∧¬W2=0W_1 \land \lnot W_2 = 0W1​∧¬W2​=0 for every input.

The proof needs only the nesting, not the exact R15–R17 values. The PCB layout also shows resistors in the R28–R38 range that the schematic image does not explain, so check the built board: probe the CD4052 A and B select pins, and watch whether D0 leaves 1.65 V, while the input sits inside window 1.

There are two fixes:

  1. Change the logic. Make the select lines encode the inner window and the ring separately: SA=W1S_A = W_1SA​=W1​, SB=W2∧¬W1S_B = W_2 \land \lnot W_1SB​=W2​∧¬W1​. Because W1⇒W2W_1 \Rightarrow W_2W1​⇒W2​, this equals W2⊕W1W_2 \oplus W_1W2​⊕W1​, so one extra XOR gate does it (both gates of U4 are already used). Inside window 1 the mux then picks channel 1 (Y1, stage 1), in the ring it picks channel 2 (Y2, stage 2), and outside both it picks channel 0.
  2. Change the wiring. Leave the logic alone and move stage 1's input from Y1 to Y3. This needs only a trace change, no extra gate.

T4.5 Software band selection and the consistency test

The XIAO cannot see SAS_ASA​, SBS_BSB​ or MUXEN, so the firmware decides which stage to trust from the readings alone. Every AUTO sample uses the same read sequence, so every sample takes the same time (T4.9):

  1. Read D2 to get x0x_0x0​ (slot 0).
  2. Read every enabled stage, highest ∣gb∣|g_b|∣gb​∣ first: stage 1 in slot 1, stage 2 in slot 2.
  3. Read D2 again to get x1x_1x1​ (slot msm_sms​, here 3).
  4. For each stage in that order, take the direct reading interpolated to the stage's own slot kkk, xk=x0+(x1−x0) k/msx_k = x_0 + (x_1 - x_0)\,k/m_sxk​=x0​+(x1​−x0​)k/ms​, and accept the stage if all of these hold:
    • xkx_kxk​ lies in the stage's window [lob−0.05, hib+0.05][\text{lo}_b - 0.05,\ \text{hi}_b + 0.05][lob​−0.05, hib​+0.05] V and not inside its hole (below);
    • yby_byb​ lies within the ADC's linear range, 0.10-3.00 V (2.45 V on a C3);
    • yby_byb​ is not at the idle level, ∣yb−idle∣≥0.1|y_b - \text{idle}| \ge 0.1∣yb​−idle∣≥0.1 V, unless CAL BANDS has confirmed that the stage is driven on both sides of its idle point;
    • the reconstruction agrees with the direct path:
∣ yb−offbgb−(x0+(x1−x0) kms)∣≤0.04 V\left|\, \frac{y_b - \text{off}_b}{g_b} - \left(x_0 + (x_1 - x_0)\,\frac{k}{m_s}\right) \right| \le 0.04\,\text{V}​gb​yb​−offb​​−(x0​+(x1​−x0​)ms​k​)​≤0.04V

The first accepted stage supplies the output, with band 1 or 2. If no stage is accepted, the output is x0x_0x0​, with band 0.

Why interpolate the direct reads. The conversions happen one after another, roughly δ\deltaδ apart, so the stage in slot kkk samples the signal at t0+kδt_0 + k\deltat0​+kδ while the two D2 reads bracket it at t0t_0t0​ and t0+msδt_0 + m_s\deltat0​+ms​δ. Linear interpolation between them is exact for any straight-line signal. For a curved one the error is the standard interpolation remainder:

xk−x(t0+kδ)=k (ms−k)2 δ2 x¨(ξ),t0<ξ<t0+msδx_k - x(t_0 + k\delta) = \frac{k\,(m_s-k)}{2}\,\delta^2\,\ddot x(\xi), \qquad t_0 < \xi < t_0 + m_s\deltaxk​−x(t0​+kδ)=2k(ms​−k)​δ2x¨(ξ),t0​<ξ<t0​+ms​δ

For a sine of peak amplitude VpV_pVp​ and angular frequency ω\omegaω, the worst-case mismatch therefore falls from VpωkδV_p\omega k\deltaVp​ωkδ (comparing with x0x_0x0​ alone) to k(ms−k)Vpω2δ2/2k(m_s-k)V_p\omega^2\delta^2/2k(ms​−k)Vp​ω2δ2/2. With ms=3m_s = 3ms​=3, both slots have k(ms−k)=2k(m_s-k) = 2k(ms​−k)=2. Take δ=15 μs\delta = 15\,\mu\text{s}δ=15μs (assumed, from the 10-20 µs per read), VpV_pVp​ = 0.5 V and 1 kHz. Comparing with x0x_0x0​ alone would give 47 mV for stage 1 and 94 mV for stage 2, both beyond the 40 mV tolerance. With interpolation both are 4.4 mV. At this amplitude the tolerance is reached at 849 Hz (stage 1) or 424 Hz (stage 2) without interpolation, and at about 3.0 kHz with it.

Why the test is robust to the Y3 problem. Every sample falls into one of three cases:

  • Stage driven and calibrated. The two estimates agree to within noise plus calibration error, so the stage is accepted.
  • Stage clipped. The linear-range check rejects it.
  • Stage idle (its channel is off). No current flows in RinR_{\text{in}}Rin​, so the output sits at yb=Vref2y_b = V_{\text{ref2}}yb​=Vref2​, the idle level that CAL ZERO measures. That reconstructs to the constant input x0,b=(Vref2−offb)/gbx_{0,b} = (V_{\text{ref2}} - \text{off}_b)/g_bx0,b​=(Vref2​−offb​)/gb​, which is within a few tens of millivolts of 0 V. Without further checks, an idle stage would pass whenever ∣xk−x0,b∣≤0.04|x_k - x_{0,b}| \le 0.04∣xk​−x0,b​∣≤0.04 V, and a small signal would be replaced by a flat line labelled as a stage.

Two rules close that last case. First, a reading at the idle level is rejected unless CAL BANDS saw the stage driven on both sides of its idle point. Near x0,bx_{0,b}x0,b​ a driven stage also reads close to idle, so only that observation can distinguish the two. Second, each stage has a hole: an input range inside its window where the mux never drives it. For nested windows that is window 1 for stage 2. The firmware does not try a stage inside its hole (shrunk by the 0.05 V margin). The default hole for stage 2 is ±0.275 V, and CAL BANDS measures both holes on the real board (T4.6).

With these rules, an accepted stage always agrees with the direct reading to within the tolerance, so the auto path is never worse than the direct path by more than 0.04 V. On the board as drawn, stage 2 is used in the ring of window 2 wherever it is not clipped (T4.3). Inside window 1 both stages are idle, so the output falls back to the direct reading.

The AUTO value comes from the slot that produced it, so its effective sampling instant is one read time (stage 1) or two (stage 2) after the direct path's. That offset is fixed for each band. Removing it would mean subtracting a slope estimated from the D2 reads, which adds the direct path's noise back into the stage reading and cancels its advantage.

T4.6 Calibration as least squares

Two-point calibration (direct and ADS8681 paths). A straight line has two unknowns, so two known inputs determine it. CAL ZERO (input shorted) averages many readings to get mid, and CAL GAIN applies a known DC voltage VVV:

mid=V‾reading∣Vin=0,g=V‾reading∣Vin=V−midV,σgg≈σmid2+σV‾2V2+(σVV)2\text{mid} = \overline{V}_{\text{reading}}\big|_{V_{\text{in}}=0}, \qquad g = \frac{\overline{V}_{\text{reading}}\big|_{V_{\text{in}}=V} - \text{mid}}{V}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_g}{g} \approx \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\text{mid}}^2 + \sigma_{\overline V}^2}{V^2} + \left(\frac{\sigma_V}{V}\right)^2}mid=Vreading​​Vin​=0​,g=VVreading​​Vin​=V​−mid​,gσg​​≈V2σmid2​+σV2​​+(VσV​​)2​

Because g≈1g \approx 1g≈1, the relative gain error is roughly the combined error of the two averages divided by VVV, plus the relative error of the known voltage itself. The first part falls as 1/V1/V1/V, so calibrate with as large a VVV as the path's range allows. For example, if each average is good to 1 mV (illustrative), VVV = 0.500 V gives about 0.28 %. The direct path must stay inside the ESP32 ADC's linear range, though. On the ESP32-C3, +1.000 V would put D2 at 2.65 V, above its roughly 2.5 V ceiling, so CAL GAIN refuses a direct-path reading outside 0.10-2.45 V (3.00 V on other chips) and prints the usable input range: about −1.50 V to +0.75 V on a C3. CAL ZERO also records the stage idle level as the mean of D1. With the input shorted, the signal sits inside window 1, where stage 2 is never driven.

CAL BANDS (gain stages). Here the input is a slowly varying signal (≤ 10 Hz) swept across at least ±1 V; CAL BANDS refuses to change anything if the input covered less than 0.5 V. Each sample gives a pair (xi,yi)(x_i, y_i)(xi​,yi​), where xix_ixi​ is the mean of the two D2 reads and yiy_iyi​ is the stage output. A sample counts as active when yiy_iyi​ is not clipped and ∣yi−idle∣>0.1|y_i - \text{idle}| > 0.1∣yi​−idle∣>0.1 V. This skips inputs within 0.1 V / G of x0x_0x0​: 18 mV for stage 1 and 42 mV for stage 2.

The firmware fits the line y=off+g xy = \text{off} + g\,xy=off+gx to the mmm active samples (mmm rather than nnn, which is the record length). It minimises the squared error, and setting both partial derivatives to zero gives two linear equations, the normal equations:

S(off,g)=∑i=1m(yi−off−g xi)2,∂S∂ off=∂S∂g=0  ⇒  {m off+g Sx=Syoff Sx+g Sxx=SxyS(\text{off}, g) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(y_i - \text{off} - g\,x_i\right)^2, \qquad \frac{\partial S}{\partial\,\text{off}} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial g} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \begin{cases} m\,\text{off} + g\,S_x = S_y \\ \text{off}\,S_x + g\,S_{xx} = S_{xy} \end{cases}S(off,g)=i=1∑m​(yi​−off−gxi​)2,∂off∂S​=∂g∂S​=0⇒{moff+gSx​=Sy​offSx​+gSxx​=Sxy​​

Here Sx=∑xiS_x = \sum x_iSx​=∑xi​, Sy=∑yiS_y = \sum y_iSy​=∑yi​, Sxx=∑xi2S_{xx} = \sum x_i^2Sxx​=∑xi2​, Sxy=∑xiyiS_{xy} = \sum x_i y_iSxy​=∑xi​yi​ and Syy=∑yi2S_{yy} = \sum y_i^2Syy​=∑yi2​. All five can be accumulated as running sums in one pass. Accumulate them in double precision, because mSxx−Sx2m S_{xx} - S_x^2mSxx​−Sx2​ subtracts two large, similar numbers. Solving the two equations gives closed forms:

g=m Sxy−SxSym Sxx−Sx2,off=Sy−g Sxm,σr=Syy−off Sy−g Sxymg = \frac{m\,S_{xy} - S_x S_y}{m\,S_{xx} - S_x^2}, \qquad \text{off} = \frac{S_y - g\,S_x}{m}, \qquad \sigma_r = \sqrt{\frac{S_{yy} - \text{off}\,S_y - g\,S_{xy}}{m}}g=mSxx​−Sx2​mSxy​−Sx​Sy​​,off=mSy​−gSx​​,σr​=mSyy​−offSy​−gSxy​​​

σr\sigma_rσr​ is the RMS residual; the identity under its square root holds only at the optimum. Dividing σr\sigma_rσr​ by ∣g∣|g|∣g∣ gives the fit error referred to the input. A second pass refits without points more than 3σr3\sigma_r3σr​ from the line, which removes samples caught mid-switch. The learned window is [min⁡xi,max⁡xi][\min x_i, \max x_i][minxi​,maxxi​] over the active samples. CAL BANDS takes 4000 samples at 2 kS/s (2 s). A stage with fewer than 100 active samples is reported as never driven and disabled; one with enough samples but less than 0.1 V of input span keeps its previous calibration. On the board as drawn, that is exactly what stage 1 should report (T4.4).

Finding the hole. The fit predicts where a driven stage should read, y^i=off+g xi\hat y_i = \text{off} + g\,x_iy^​i​=off+gxi​. A sample inside the learned window that reads idle, ∣yi−idle∣<0.1|y_i - \text{idle}| < 0.1∣yi​−idle∣<0.1 V, although the fit puts it well away from idle, ∣y^i−idle∣>0.2|\hat y_i - \text{idle}| > 0.2∣y^​i​−idle∣>0.2 V, can only come from an input where the mux is not driving the stage. The hole is the range of those inputs, if there are at least five. For stage 2 with nested windows, that is window 1. The stage counts as driven around its idle point ("trusted near idle", T4.5) when active samples lie on both sides of x0,bx_{0,b}x0,b​ and x0,bx_{0,b}x0,b​ is not in a hole. This test looks only at samples that contradict the fit. Inferring holes from gaps between active samples instead would give false holes whenever the sweep frequency divides the 2 kS/s sampling rate, because the samples then land on the same few input values every cycle.

Two smaller effects are negligible:

  • Noise in xxx. Noise in the input variable shrinks a least-squares slope by the factor Var⁡(x)/(Var⁡(x)+σx2)\operatorname{Var}(x)/(\operatorname{Var}(x) + \sigma_x^2)Var(x)/(Var(x)+σx2​). Assume 5 mV rms per read (3.5 mV after averaging two) and a sweep that is uniform over the window. The slope is then low by 0.05 % for stage 1 (once it is driven) and 0.005 % for stage 2.
  • Read order. CAL BANDS reads D2, D0, D1, D2, so the D2 average is centred between D0 and D1 and each stage is off-centre by half a read-time, δ/2\delta/2δ/2. The first-order skew is reduced but not cancelled. For a slow sweep, such as a 1 Hz, ±1.5 V triangle (6 V/s), it amounts to 6 V/s × 7.5 µs = 45 µV.

T4.7 Edge trigger with hysteresis

A plain rule such as "fire when x≥Lx \ge Lx≥L" also fires on noise: when the signal hovers near LLL, or falls slowly through it, noise creates extra upward crossings at the wrong phase. The displayed trace then jumps between alignments. The firmware instead uses a two-state machine, a software Schmitt trigger. For a rising edge with level LLL and hysteresis hhh (the falling edge is mirrored):

armed←1  if x[k]<L−h;fire if armed∧x[k]≥L, then armed←0\text{armed} \leftarrow 1 \ \text{ if } x[k] < L - h; \qquad \text{fire if } \text{armed} \land x[k] \ge L, \ \text{then armed} \leftarrow 0armed←1  if x[k]<L−h;fire if armed∧x[k]≥L, then armed←0

A false trigger now needs one sample below L−hL - hL−h and a later one at or above LLL while the true signal is not rising. The noise on the two samples must therefore cover at least hhh between them. For independent Gaussian noise of rms σ\sigmaσ, the most likely split is h/2h/2h/2 each, which gives a bound for any one such pair of samples (for hhh well above σ\sigmaσ):

Pfalse, per pair≤Q ⁣(h2σ)2P_{\text{false, per pair}} \le Q\!\left(\frac{h}{2\sigma}\right)^{2}Pfalse, per pair​≤Q(2σh​)2

QQQ is the Gaussian tail probability. With the default hhh = 30 mV and an assumed σ\sigmaσ = 5 mV, the bound is Q(3)2≈1.8×10−6Q(3)^2 \approx 1.8\times10^{-6}Q(3)2≈1.8×10−6. At σ\sigmaσ = 10 mV it rises to 4.5×10−34.5\times10^{-3}4.5×10−3, and without hysteresis it is 1/4. A fast edge crosses the band in a sample or two and offers few such pairs. A slow or flat signal parked inside the band offers many, and it will eventually false-trigger. Keep hhh above about 6.6σ6.6\sigma6.6σ (the rule of T3.8), which for the default 30 mV means noise below about 4.5 mV rms, and set LLL away from flat parts of the waveform. The cost is that a signal must dip at least hhh below LLL before it can trigger at all.

The trigger fires on the first sample at or above LLL, without interpolation. For a signal unrelated to the sample clock, the displayed trigger point therefore jitters uniformly over one sample period, with rms T/12T/\sqrt{12}T/12​ = 28.9 µs at 10 kS/s. The level LLL is in reconstructed probe volts (default 0 V). The trigger modes are FREE (no trigger), AUTO (sends an untriggered record if no trigger arrives in time), NORMAL (waits for a trigger) and SINGLE (one triggered record, then stop).

T4.8 Pre-trigger ring buffer

While waiting for a trigger, samples go into an nnn-sample ring at write index www, which increments mod nnn. The number of pre-trigger samples is pre=⌊np/100⌋\text{pre} = \lfloor n p / 100 \rfloorpre=⌊np/100⌋, and a trigger is accepted only once at least pre samples exist. If the trigger sample is written at index wtw_twt​, the firmware takes n−pre−1n - \text{pre} - 1n−pre−1 more samples. The ring is then full, so the next write index also holds the oldest sample, and rotating the buffer to start there puts the trigger at a fixed position:

wend=(wt+n−pre) mod n,out[j]=buf[(wend+j) mod n],jt=(wt−wend) mod n=prew_{\text{end}} = (w_t + n - \text{pre}) \bmod n, \qquad \text{out}[j] = \text{buf}[(w_{\text{end}} + j) \bmod n], \qquad j_t = (w_t - w_{\text{end}}) \bmod n = \text{pre}wend​=(wt​+n−pre)modn,out[j]=buf[(wend​+j)modn],jt​=(wt​−wend​)modn=pre

The trigger therefore always appears at index pre, wherever the ring happened to be. With the defaults nnn = 1000 and ppp = 25 %, pre = 250. At 10 kS/s that gives 25.0 ms before the trigger and 74.9 ms after it, in a 100 ms record. For nnn = 4096, pre = 1024.

T4.9 Sample timing: pacing, measured rate and ADS8681 alignment

The loop waits for the CPU cycle counter to reach the next tick, spaced ⌊fCPU/fs⌋\lfloor f_{\text{CPU}}/f_s \rfloor⌊fCPU​/fs​⌋ cycles apart: 16 000 cycles at 160 MHz (C3, C6) or 24 000 cycles at 240 MHz (S3), for 10 kS/s. Each mode costs a fixed number of native reads per sample: one for DIRECT and four for AUTO with both stages (T4.5), plus an ADS8681 frame for EXT and ALL. Before each capture the firmware times four dry-run samples and paces no faster than the slowest one plus 12.5 %. At an assumed 15 µs per read that caps AUTO at about 14.8 kS/s and DIRECT at about 59 kS/s; a faster request runs at the cap with evenly spaced samples. The firmware timestamps the first and last samples with the 1 µs system timer and sends the measured rate, where nacqn_{\text{acq}}nacq​ is the number of samples in that acquisition (including those overwritten in the ring while waiting):

fs=nacq−1tlast−tfirstf_s = \frac{n_{\text{acq}} - 1}{t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{first}}}fs​=tlast​−tfirst​nacq​−1​

The 1 µs timestamp resolution contributes about 10 ppm over a 99.9 ms record. This is an average rate, so it does not reveal sample-to-sample jitter caused by interrupts; after a delayed sample the loop shortens the next interval to return to the grid. The host scales every time and frequency by this fsf_sfs​, so any error in it passes straight into the readouts.

ADS8681 pipeline. The ADS8681 samples on the rising edge of CONVST/CS and shifts that result out during the next SPI frame. The code read in tick kkk therefore belongs to tick k−1k-1k−1, a one-sample delay, z−1z^{-1}z−1. Left alone, the ADS8681 trace in MODE ALL would lag the native traces by TTT, which is 36° of phase at 1 kHz and 10 kS/s. The firmware primes one conversion before the capture and delays the native readings by one sample in software, so both paths carry the same z−1z^{-1}z−1:

stored[k]=( ynative[k−1], yads[k] ),yads[k]=Q16 ⁣(Vin(tCS,k−1))\text{stored}[k] = \big(\,y_{\text{native}}[k-1],\ y_{\text{ads}}[k]\,\big), \qquad y_{\text{ads}}[k] = Q_{16}\!\left(V_{\text{in}}(t_{\text{CS},k-1})\right)stored[k]=(ynative​[k−1], yads​[k]),yads​[k]=Q16​(Vin​(tCS,k−1​))

Here Q16Q_{16}Q16​ is the 16-bit quantizer of T4.1. What remains is the short gap between the CS edge and the first native read in the same tick, at most about one read time δ\deltaδ. On top of that, the EXT signal lags by the group delay of the ADS8681's internal filter, about 14 µs at low frequency (T1.5), which no sample alignment removes.

T4.10 Host measurements

For a record y0…yn−1y_0 \dots y_{n-1}y0​…yn−1​, the host computes the basic statistics. Its RMS includes the DC component, and AC RMS follows from it:

yˉ=1n∑yi,RMS=1n∑yi2,AC RMS=RMS2−yˉ2,pk-pk=max⁡yi−min⁡yi\bar y = \frac{1}{n}\sum y_i, \qquad \text{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum y_i^2}, \qquad \text{AC RMS} = \sqrt{\text{RMS}^2 - \bar y^2}, \qquad \text{pk-pk} = \max y_i - \min y_iyˉ​=n1​∑yi​,RMS=n1​∑yi2​​,AC RMS=RMS2−yˉ​2​,pk-pk=maxyi​−minyi​

For example, a 0.5 V-amplitude sine on 0.2 V DC reads 0.406 V RMS, of which 0.354 V is AC. A record seldom holds a whole number of cycles. For a sine spanning KKK cycles, the partial cycle changes the RMS by at most about 1/(4πK)1/(4\pi K)1/(4πK): 0.8 % at 10 cycles and 0.08 % at 100. Noise biases pk-pk upward. For pure Gaussian noise of rms σ\sigmaσ, the expected max − min of 1000 samples is about 6.5σ6.5\sigma6.5σ (about 7.3σ7.3\sigma7.3σ for 4096). A flat trace with an assumed 5 mV of noise therefore reads about 32 mV pk-pk.

Frequency comes from rising crossings of the mid-level vmid=(max⁡+min⁡)/2v_{\text{mid}} = (\max + \min)/2vmid​=(max+min)/2, with 10 % of pk-pk as hysteresis. The detector re-arms below vmid−0.1 pk-pkv_{\text{mid}} - 0.1\,\text{pk-pk}vmid​−0.1pk-pk, the same logic as T4.7. A crossing between samples iii and i+1i+1i+1 is located by linear interpolation. The period uses only the first and last of the kkk crossings, and at least two crossings are needed:

tc=i+vmid−yiyi+1−yi (samples),P^=clast−cfirst(k−1) fs,f^=1P^t_c = i + \frac{v_{\text{mid}} - y_i}{y_{i+1} - y_i}\ \text{(samples)}, \qquad \hat P = \frac{c_{\text{last}} - c_{\text{first}}}{(k-1)\,f_s}, \qquad \hat f = \frac{1}{\hat P}tc​=i+yi+1​−yi​vmid​−yi​​ (samples),P^=(k−1)fs​clast​−cfirst​​,f^​=P^1​

Noise of rms σv\sigma_vσv​ shifts each crossing in time by about σv\sigma_vσv​ divided by the slope there, which is VpωV_p\omegaVp​ω for a sine. Only the two end crossings enter the estimate, so their error is spread over the whole span D=(clast−cfirst)/fsD = (c_{\text{last}} - c_{\text{first}})/f_sD=(clast​−cfirst​)/fs​:

σt≈σvVp ω,σff≈2 σtD\sigma_t \approx \frac{\sigma_v}{V_p\,\omega}, \qquad \frac{\sigma_f}{f} \approx \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_t}{D}σt​≈Vp​ωσv​​,fσf​​≈D2​σt​​

As an example, take a 1 kHz sine of 0.5 V amplitude with an assumed σv\sigma_vσv​ = 5 mV, sampled at fsf_sfs​ = 10 kS/s with nnn = 1000. That gives kkk ≈ 100 crossings, DDD ≈ 99 ms, σt\sigma_tσt​ = 1.6 µs and σf\sigma_fσf​ ≈ 0.023 Hz. A software simulation running the host's own function on synthetic noisy sines gave about 0.020 Hz. The simulated figure is slightly lower because each interpolated point blends two samples, which partly averages their noise.

Without noise, interpolation is very accurate at a sine's mid-level crossing, because the curvature there is zero. At 10 samples per cycle the error is at most 0.0065 samples (0.65 µs). In practice, error in fsf_sfs​ (T4.9) and aliasing (there is no anti-aliasing filter ahead of the ESP32 pins) matter more than either effect.

T4.11 AC coupling and duty cycle

Hardware AC coupling does not work on this input as it stands. A series capacitor CCC into the board's load (T1.6: RLR_LRL​ = 19.6 kΩ to VthV_\text{th}Vth​ = 1.649 V) forms a high-pass filter:

H(s)=sRLC1+sRLC,fc=12πRLC(C=1 μF⇒fc=8.1 Hz)H(s) = \frac{sR_LC}{1 + sR_LC}, \qquad f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R_L C} \quad (C = 1\,\mu\text{F} \Rightarrow f_c = 8.1\,\text{Hz})H(s)=1+sRL​CsRL​C​,fc​=2πRL​C1​(C=1μF⇒fc​=8.1Hz)

But the capacitor also removes the DC path from the source, so RawInput settles to VthV_\text{th}Vth​ = 1.649 V, the top of the range, and the signal clips. A resistor RgR_gRg​ to GND only pulls the operating point down to VthRg/(Rg+RL)V_\text{th}R_g/(R_g + R_L)Vth​Rg​/(Rg​+RL​). Staying under 10 mV needs Rg≤R_g \leRg​≤ 120 Ω, which then loads the source through CCC. On this board, AC coupling belongs in software, or behind a buffer that has its own ground-referenced bias.

Software AC coupling. Subtracting the record mean is exact for a whole number of cycles; it is the AC RMS of T4.10. For a live trace, a running first-order digital high-pass also works:

y[k]=a (y[k−1]+x[k]−x[k−1]),a=ττ+T,fc≈12πτ(τ≫T)y[k] = a\,\big(y[k-1] + x[k] - x[k-1]\big), \qquad a = \frac{\tau}{\tau + T}, \qquad f_c \approx \frac{1}{2\pi\tau} \quad (\tau \gg T)y[k]=a(y[k−1]+x[k]−x[k−1]),a=τ+Tτ​,fc​≈2πτ1​(τ≫T)

Any high-pass tilts a square wave. Over a flat half-period tht_hth​ the level decays by 1−e−th/τ≈th/τ1 - e^{-t_h/\tau} \approx t_h/\tau1−e−th​/τ≈th​/τ. For 1 % tilt on a 10 Hz square wave (tht_hth​ = 50 ms) that means τ≥\tau \geτ≥ 5 s, or fc≤f_c \lefc​≤ 0.032 Hz.

Duty cycle moves the baseline. After AC coupling, a pulse train of height VVV and duty cycle DDD has zero mean, so it sits at (1−D)V(1 - D)V(1−D)V and −DV-DV−DV. A rising trigger at LLL = 0 V with hysteresis hhh only re-arms if the low level goes below −h-h−h, that is if DV>hDV > hDV>h. With the default hhh = 30 mV and VVV = 1 V, pulses with DDD < 3 % would never trigger. The firmware triggers on DC-coupled samples, so this only matters if AC coupling is ever moved into the firmware.

Measuring duty cycle. Using the same interpolated mid-level crossings as T4.10, D=(tfall−trise)/PD = (t_\text{fall} - t_\text{rise})/PD=(tfall​−trise​)/P. For edges much faster than TTT, interpolation cannot help, and each edge is only known to within one sample period. Two independent uniform errors give, per cycle:

σD=T6 P\sigma_D = \frac{T}{\sqrt{6}\,P}σD​=6​PT​

That is 4.1 percentage points for a 1 kHz square wave at 10 kS/s. Averaging KKK cycles divides the error by K\sqrt{K}K​ (0.41 points over 100 cycles), but only if the sample phase drifts from cycle to cycle. When fsf_sfs​ is an exact multiple of fff the phases repeat, and the error becomes a fixed bias of up to T/PT/PT/P. The host does not compute duty cycle yet; this is what such a measurement would deliver.

T4.12 CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE

Each packet carries a 16-bit CRC over the type, version, length and payload fields; the A5 5A sync word is not covered. The CRC treats the bit string as a polynomial over GF(2), where coefficients are 0 or 1 and addition is XOR. The checksum is the remainder after dividing by a fixed generator polynomial:

G(x)=x16+x12+x5+1    (0x1021),R(x)=x16 M′(x) mod G(x)G(x) = x^{16} + x^{12} + x^5 + 1 \;\; (\texttt{0x1021}), \qquad R(x) = x^{16}\, M'(x) \bmod G(x)G(x)=x16+x12+x5+1(0x1021),R(x)=x16M′(x)modG(x)

M′(x)M'(x)M′(x) is the message with its first 16 bits inverted. That inversion is the effect of the 0xFFFF initial value, and it makes leading zero bytes count. The receiver recomputes the CRC and compares, so an error pattern E(x)E(x)E(x) goes undetected only if G(x)G(x)G(x) divides it. Over GF(2), G(x)=(x+1)(x15+x14+x13+x12+x4+x3+x2+x+1)G(x) = (x+1)(x^{15}+x^{14}+x^{13}+x^{12}+x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1)G(x)=(x+1)(x15+x14+x13+x12+x4+x3+x2+x+1), and the degree-15 factor is primitive, with order 215−1=327672^{15}-1 = 32767215−1=32767. The guarantees follow from this factorization:

Error pattern Detected? Why
any single bit always the only divisors of xix^ixi are powers of xxx, and G(0)=1G(0) = 1G(0)=1
any odd number of bits always G(1)=0G(1) = 0G(1)=0 so (x+1)(x+1)(x+1) divides GGG, but E(1)=1E(1) = 1E(1)=1
two bits ddd apart unless ddd is a multiple of 32767 GGG divides xd+1x^d + 1xd+1 only when 32767 divides ddd
burst of length 16 or less always E=xiB(x)E = x^i B(x)E=xiB(x) with deg⁡B<16\deg B < 16degB<16 and G(0)=1G(0) = 1G(0)=1
burst of exactly 17 bits all but 2−15≈3.1×10−52^{-15} \approx 3.1\times10^{-5}2−15≈3.1×10−5 standard CRC burst result
longer bursts, random patterns all but 2−16≈1.5×10−52^{-16} \approx 1.5\times10^{-5}2−16≈1.5×10−5 one remainder in 2162^{16}216 is zero

Within 32 767 bits (4093 data bytes plus the CRC), every 1-, 2- and 3-bit error is caught, which is a Hamming distance of 4. With the current packet layout (the 6 CRC-covered header bytes, type, version and length, plus a 28-byte waveform header; the A5 5A sync word is outside the CRC), a single-channel frame fits up to 1014 samples. The default 1000-sample single-channel frame covers 4034 bytes. An AUTO frame with band codes (5034 bytes) or a three-channel MODE ALL frame (13 034 bytes) is longer. In those, two flipped bits a multiple of 32 767 bits apart would pass undetected, and every other row of the table still holds. Python's binascii.crc_hqx(data, 0xFFFF) computes the same CRC, and the standard check string "123456789" gives 0x29B1.

Sources

Datasheet and documentation values used in this chapter. Typical values are typical; check the current revision of each document for your parts.

  • ADS8681: TI datasheet SBAS633 (PDF). Used for the internal anti-aliasing filter (−3 dB at 15 kHz, −0.1 dB at 2.5 kHz), input impedance, SNR and SINAD per range, the range register and the output coding. Two TI E2E answers cover the one-frame result latency and the unpublished filter transfer function.
  • TSV794: ST datasheet DS13480 (PDF). Used for gain-bandwidth (50 MHz typical, 35 MHz minimum), slew rate, voltage noise and offset, all characterised at 5 V.
  • CD4052B: TI product page and datasheet. Used for on-resistance versus supply and the 3–20 V supply range.
  • MCP6541/2/3/4: Microchip datasheet (mirror). Used for internal hysteresis, input offset and propagation delay.
  • ESP32-C3 / ESP32-S3 ADC: Espressif ESP-IDF ADC guides for the C3 and S3, Espressif's 2025 ADC performance comparison, and the Arduino-ESP32 ADC API. Used for the calibrated input ranges, DNL/INL and analogReadMilliVolts().
  • CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE: parameter set (poly 0x1021, init 0xFFFF, check 0x29B1), e.g. the RIOT OS reference.

6What I did

Analog & circuit design

Designed the level-shifting front end, the window-comparator ladder, the per-window gain stages, and clamp / fault-current protection. Verified matched-resistor gain relationships and power-vs-signal pin separation in simulation before committing to layout.

PCB design & fabrication

Laid out a two-layer board in KiCad. Diagnosed a footprint-library mismatch on the ADS8681 (TSSOP-16), cleared DRC violations (unconnected nets, missing board outline, dangling tracks and vias), verified the Gerber and Excellon export, and hand-soldered the board, including fine-pitch TSSOP-16 and SOIC parts.

Firmware

Wrote an SPI driver for the ADS8681 from scratch, since no Arduino library supports the ADS868x family. Implemented the direct-ADC path and the window-detection and voltage-reconstruction logic that recovers the true input from each sampled window.

Data acquisition & visualization

Built a Python app that streams samples over serial and plots them in real time with LightningChart Python's GPU-accelerated charts.
